We develop a statistical prediction for the mean flip rate in terms of phase-space flux. Applying this flux-based approach to the equal-mass, equal-arm ("egalitarian") double pendulum, we find excellent agreement between the statistical prediction and numerical simulations: ensemble-averaged flip rates agree to within 1%, while even the statistics of individual chaotic trajectories agree at the few-percent level, quantifying the validity of the ergodic approximation. This agreement holds for flips of either arm and over a broad range of energies. This flux-based approach is closely related to that used for the egalitarian three-body system. A central role is played by the saddle orbits: periodic orbits that tend to the periodic saddle eigenmode as the energy approaches the saddle energy from above and approximately follow the ridge of the potential at higher energies. These orbits provide a natural dividing surface for defining flips while avoiding recrossings. Indeed, the resulting distribution of crossing times exhibits a distinct gap. It is argued that the corresponding flux-over-a-saddle prediction provides a preferred realization of the flux-based approach. We also present two simplified alternative dividing surfaces, including one based on a remarkably accurate analytic approximation to the saddle orbits, and show that both yield statistical predictions in agreement with the corresponding simulated rates.

papers.title: A Layered Simplex Architecture for Large Alphabets
papers.abstract: A learning architecture induces a prior over its expressible models. Recent work links architectural success to a broad complexity spectrum: model probabilities spanning many orders of magnitude. Understanding how depth shapes these priors and prediction may help explain the success of neural networks and transformers. We study this connection in large-alphabet prediction through the *layered simplex architecture* (LSA), which multiplies independent uniform simplex vectors coordinate-wise and normalizes. At depth zero, the prior is concentrated on the uniform distribution; at depth one, the Bayesian predictor is Laplace's rule. Each additional layer shifts prior mass toward more concentrated distributions. We derive exact Bayesian marginal likelihood and regret expressions using reusable depth-specific kernels. Mixing over depths up to a cutoff logarithmic in alphabet size yields an explicit predictor with rigorous guarantees. For targets uniform on a specified sparse support, the mixture's prior complexity is asymptotic to the support-description cost at every fixed positive KL resolution, establishing a broad complexity spectrum. We also prove a regret lower bound for every label-invariant predictor: the expected description length of the discovered symbol set minus the source's uncertainty about its identity given its size. For Zipf sources in a growing-alphabet regime, the depth mixture attains this bound to leading order. Thus, the symbol-discovery rate determines the regret exponent. Although introduced to study depth, the LSA predictor competes with established large-alphabet methods, including Good--Turing, Ristad's law and an adaptive Dirichlet mixture, while substantially outperforming classical add-constant rules on concentrated sources.

papers.title: Estimation of the cumulant $b_4$ and sextic self-coupling of the QCD axion at finite temperature and density
papers.abstract: The sixth-order cumulant $b_4$ of the QCD topological charge distribution and the axion's sextic self-coupling at finite temperature $T$ and baryon chemical potential $\mu$ are calculated within the two-flavor quark-meson (QM) model without and with the Polyakov-loop dynamics. The $b_4$ in the vacuum falls within the range predicted by lattice SU(3) pure-gauge simulations, and at large $T$ and/or $\mu$, it tends to a constant predicted by the dilute instanton gas approximation. Both $b_4$ and the axion's sextic self-coupling diverge at the QCD critical point and flip sign across the phase transition. The range of accuracy of the fourth- and sixth-order Taylor expansions of the free energy as a function of the $\theta$ parameter is investigated via comparison with the full potential at the mean-field level.

papers.title: Experimental High-Dimensional Quantum Overlapping Tomography
papers.abstract: Large-scale quantum systems have advanced rapidly via the exploration of more particles and higher dimensions, offering great potential for developing quantum technologies. However, their characterization becomes prohibitive with increasing local dimensionality and particle number. Here we propose high-dimensional quantum overlapping tomography based on a graph-theoretic formulation, which allows one to efficiently reconstruct few-body marginals of multipartite high-dimensional quantum systems. We experimentally realize it on a photonic four-party entangled state in a $4 \times 4 \times 2 \times 2$ system. Using measurements in mutually unbiased bases, we reconstruct all six two-body marginals with only 25 projective measurement settings, compared with 94 and 225 settings for independent tomography of all two-body reduced states and full state tomography, respectively. The reconstructed marginals reveal a layered entanglement structure vital for high-dimensional quantum networks. We further show that these marginals enable more noise-resilient certification of multipartite high-dimensional entanglement than the fidelity-based criterion. Our work thus offers a scalable route for learning multidimensional quantum systems.

papers.title: TEA: Text Encoder Alignment for Robust Concept Erasure in Text-to-Image Models
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can be misused to generate harmful content through adversarial or paraphrased prompts that bypass built-in safety mechanisms. Existing concept erasure methods often suffer from limited robustness against adversarial prompts, degradation of benign generation quality, or reliance on inference-time interventions that introduce persistent computational overhead. To address these limitations, we formulate concept erasure as a domain alignment problem in the text representation space. We propose a lightweight Text Encoder Alignment framework (TEA) that fine-tunes only the text encoder while keeping the generative backbone fully frozen. Given concept-anchor prompt pairs, our method trains a discriminator to distinguish token-level representations of concept-bearing prompts from those of safe anchor prompts, while updating the text encoder to make these representations indistinguishable. TEA introduces zero inference-time overhead and trains in seconds with only a few fine-tuning steps, making it practical for large-scale deployment. Despite this efficiency, TEA achieves state-of-the-art erasure robustness against black-box and white-box adversarial attacks on Stable Diffusion v1.4, while preserving generation quality on benign prompts. Furthermore, TEA is model-agnostic and achieves the lowest attack success rate on Stable Diffusion v3.5, extending concept erasure to Rectified Flow Transformer architectures with T5 conditioning, which remain largely unexplored by prior methods. Code is available at https://github.com/alirezafarashah/TEA

papers.title: de Broglie-Bohm Dynamics with Schr\"odinger Source Fields: A Framework for Subquantum Theory
papers.abstract: We extend de Broglie--Bohm (dBB) pilot-wave theory by introducing a complex source field into the Schr\"odinger equation and examining its effects on quantum equilibrium and nonequilibrium dynamics. In dBB theory, the physical particle distribution P, rather than the Born density $|{\psi}|^2$, carries the ensemble probability, so a source term may modify the pilot wave without violating conservation of total particle probability. We derive the source-modified Hamilton--Jacobi and continuity equations, the transport equation for the nonequilibrium ratio $f=P/|{\psi}|^2$, and an exact entropy-production formula. Three applications follow. First, suitably designed sources can drive exponential relaxation toward quantum equilibrium. Second, the entropy-production rate admits a Prigogine-type bilinear form, providing a basis for a subquantum thermodynamics with entropy-producing and entropy-extracting regimes. Third, a tuned source can exactly cancel the Bohmian quantum potential, yielding classical particle trajectories while the guiding wave retains nontrivial structure and the nonequilibrium ratio remains conserved. The resulting framework provides a unified setting for studying source-driven quantum nonequilibrium, entropy exchange, and classicalization, and motivates further investigation of the physical and ontological status of the source field.

papers.title: Efficient Hessian-Free Methods for Multi-Objective Bilevel Optimization with a Nonconvex Lower-Level Objective
papers.abstract: Multi-objective bilevel optimization has wide applications in the AI area such as automated learning and multi-task meta-learning. Although some recent studies have investigated multi-objective bilevel optimization, many existing methods rely on the (strongly) convex lower level problems. In fact, these multi-objective bilevel learning problems are generally nonconvex, and particularly their lower level problems are nonconvex. To fill this gap, we propose a class of Multi-Objective Moreau Envelope based Hessian-free Algorithms (MOMEHA) for the multi-objective bilevel learning problems with a nonconvex lower level. Specifically, our method uses the Moreau envelope to formulate a multi-objective single-level relaxation that enforces lower-level first-order stationarity. In particular, our method retains computational advantages of being single-loop and Hessian-free in the multi-objective setting by incorporating a smooth weighted Tchebycheff scalarization. Furthermore, we propose a momentum variant of MOMEHA (i.e., MB-MOMEHA) for the stochastic multi-objective bilevel learning problems. Under the stated assumptions, we establish finite-iteration bounds on the Moreau gap and Pareto stationarity residuals under dynamically relaxed gap constraints in both deterministic and stochastic settings. Some experiments on few-shot meta-learning and neural architecture search demonstrate that our methods outperform the existing approaches in terms of Pareto front quality, validating their effectiveness and robustness.

papers.title: Techno-Economic Boundary Analysis of Small Modular Reactor Cogeneration for Hyperscale Data Center IT and Cooling Loads
papers.abstract: Growing data-center electricity demand has increased interest in colocation with small modular reactors, but the conditions under which reactor power and steam-driven cooling reduce energy costs remain uncertain. Cooling can account for 20-40% of facility electricity use, making steam extraction a potential source of savings as well as a loss of turbine generation. We co-optimize hourly reactor dispatch, steam extraction, absorption cooling and grid exchange for a 200 MW$_\mathrm{e}$ data center in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region, using a 109-entry scenario set spanning capital, market, policy, financing and cooling efficiency. At 2023 mid-range reactor capital, the nuclear configurations cost 54.9-67.7% more than grid supply even with the Section 45Y production tax credit. With the other 2023 assumptions held fixed, cogeneration reaches grid parity near \$5000 kW$_\mathrm{e}^{-1}$. At nth-of-a-kind capital, nuclear supply is 85.9-98.7% cheaper than grid procurement in 2023, but between parity and 34.8% more expensive in the low-price 2024 market. A carbon price of \$53.1-64.0 tCO$_2^{-1}$ closes the mid-range gap when exports receive credits at the hourly average grid emission factor; the resulting negative balances are attributional and do not represent physical carbon removal. Absorption cooling responds to hourly electricity prices and supplies 32.6% of annual cooling, but adds \$9.7 million yr$^{-1}$ relative to the reactor-only plant. Absorption breaks even at an installed cost of \$26 kW$_\mathrm{c}^{-1}$ at baseline efficiency and \$529 kW$_\mathrm{c}^{-1}$ on a legacy-efficiency campus, compared with surveyed commercial prices of \$450-1200 kW$_\mathrm{c}^{-1}$.

papers.title: Lunar Reflective Interferometry
papers.abstract: We present the method of lunar reflection interferometry (LRI) in which a virtual interferometer can be formed by using a spacecraft-borne antenna in lunar orbit that receives both direct rays and those reflected from the lunar surface. The technique exploits the method of images and is akin to the classic "sea cliff" interferometer, with the Moon's surface, primarily the lunar Maria, replacing the ocean surface. We describe the method in detail, demonstrate that significant portions of the Moon's surface are sufficiently smooth at low radio frequencies, $\nu \lesssim 10\,\mathrm{MHz}$, for the technique to work, and outline a spacecraft instrument implementation. We describe potential systematic errors and how they could be mitigated. We present several astrophysics applications of the method.

papers.title: Linearized 2-Simplicial Attention
papers.abstract: We present a linearized form of 2-simplicial attention by rewriting the trilinear score as an inner product between a composite query and a key, so that the sum over keys takes the same form as ordinary softmax attention. We then approximate this sum with positive random features and store all previous keys in a fixed-size state, while the sum over second keys stays exact over all previous tokens. This reduces the cost from cubic to quadratic in sequence length, and both keys range over all previous tokens, which windowed 2-simplicial attention does not allow. We implement it with custom Triton kernels and combine it with Kimi Delta Attention to build a model with no softmax attention at all. With 15B equal training tokens on FineWeb-Edu, this model lowers validation loss from 2.35 to 2.32 over a KDA hybrid and lowers LAMBADA perplexity from 40 to 38.

papers.title: Biomedical Knowledge Composition: A Software Engineering Perspective
papers.abstract: Biomedical research has accumulated vast molecular, clinical, and population data, yet translating this wealth into actionable knowledge remains constrained by technical and organizational difficulties. This article presents a unified treatment of two perspectives on biomedical knowledge infrastructure. The first introduces the biomedical domain to software engineers: it explains why knowledge graphs (KGs) are the central integrative data structure in modern biomedicine, characterizes five data harmonization challenges (identifier mapping, entity resolution, schema alignment, evidence integration, and provenance tracking), surveys application domains from drug discovery to digital twins, and profiles six representative KG systems with contrasting choices. The second perspective asks why engineering biomedical knowledge infrastructure remains so difficult. We argue that a contributing root cause is limited adoption of software tooling and practices that make development in other mature domains - particularly web engineering - reliably composable and reproducible: package management, typed namespaces, canonical interchange formats, service composition protocols, reproducible pipelines, and lifecycle governance. Against this backdrop, eight open engineering challenges for biomedical data integration are catalogued, each with partial solutions but no universally adopted stack. Crucially, the article shifts emphasis from describing deployed KG instances toward the reproducible process of assembling them: reusable build pipelines, versioned dependencies, and engineering practices that let others compile and customize a KG from source rather than consuming a static artifact. Together, the two perspectives provide domain grounding for newcomers and a research agenda for software engineers seeking to make transformative contributions to biomedical knowledge infrastructure.

papers.title: CommitKV: Commit-Aligned KV Cache Compression for Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract: Multimodal agents gather visual evidence through reasoning and tool use, extending their ability to solve tasks beyond the initial input. However, accumulating observations increases KV cache memory and inference costs. Token eviction reduces these costs by retaining useful cached tokens. Existing methods use attention, redundancy, or stage-specific queries to rank tokens, without explicitly comparing the same history across tool interactions. When observations shift attention, they may mistake temporarily reduced influence for lost usefulness and evict information needed later. We propose CommitKV, a training-free KV cache compression method that accounts for this changing evidence use. Commit-aligned measurement compares the deletion effects of the same page before a tool call completes and after its observation returns. Lifecycle-aware compression retires pages with low influence in both windows and temporarily protects pages influential before the call. Joint scoring combines attention importance, key redundancy, and token-level deletion effects to fill the remaining budget. Extensive experiments cover four open-weight multimodal models and eight benchmarks. CommitKV achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared compression methods on all four models. On Qwen3-VL-8B, it achieves 69.85% at a 512-token budget, only 0.91% below FullKV, and exceeds the strongest compression baseline by 8.44% at 256 tokens. Deploying the Qwen3-VL-8B agent with SGLang and vLLM at a 256-token budget reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 54.37%-55.23% and accelerates end-to-end inference by 2.12-2.17$\times$ over FullKV on the matched workload.

papers.title: Projection-Retraction MPPI: Exact Command-Space Constraint-Manifold Control for Manipulators
papers.abstract: Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is widely used in manipulation for its gradient-free, parallel handling of non-convex costs. Manipulation tasks, however, often impose constraints that hold throughout the motion: a closed kinematic chain that two grasping arms keep exactly, or joint limits and obstacle clearances that are never crossed. Standard MPPI handles such constraints only through the cost, as soft penalties that hold approximately and fail under a strong task cost. To address this, we propose Projection-Retraction MPPI (PR-MPPI), which enforces the constraints inside the sampled dynamics. At every rollout step, the sampled velocity is projected to satisfy both constraint types: the equality restricts it to a subspace, and each inequality to a half-space within that subspace, so inequality handling never breaks the equality. This projection, however, satisfies the constraints only to first order, and a finite step leaves a small drift off the equality. Therefore, we retract the returned command back onto the constraint, so that the commanded configuration satisfies the equality to numerical tolerance, independently of task weighting. We validate PR-MPPI on 14-DoF dual-arm systems. In simulation, the returned commands satisfy the closed-chain equality to numerical tolerance through a joint-limit stress test and randomized obstacle avoidance, while the measured trajectories retain the joint-limit and obstacle margins. On real hardware, the arms of a Unitree H1-2 humanoid reactively avoid a moving obstacle. Code and experiment videos are available at https://rcilab.khu.ac.kr/prmppi/.

papers.title: Analytic Spread Complexity from Level Statistics: From Chaos to Integrability
papers.abstract: Spread complexity has emerged as a useful probe of quantum chaos, yet the microscopic spectral origin of its characteristic finite-time peak remains incompletely understood. We develop an analytic framework that relates spread complexity directly to local spectral statistics. Starting from an energy-space representation of the Krylov kernel, we show that the kernel is approximately banded, leading to a rapidly convergent diagonal expansion dominated by nearby levels in the ordered spectrum. Motivated by this structure, we propose an approximate kernel-universality hypothesis: after unfolding, the Krylov kernel is well approximated by that of a uniform lattice. Combining this universal kernel with local spectral statistics yields a simple analytic expression for spread complexity in terms of the Fourier transforms of the $k$-th nearest-neighbour spacing distributions. In particular, at leading order, the finite-time peak is controlled by the Fourier transform of the nearest-neighbour spacing distribution. The resulting framework describes both chaotic random-matrix ensembles and the integrable Poisson limit, identifies the spectral origin of the complexity peak and its late-time behaviour, and provides a direct connection between Krylov dynamics and spectral statistics.

papers.title: What Should Visual Place Recognition Be Invariant To? Rethinking Condition Invariance in Visual Place Recognition
papers.abstract: Condition invariance in Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is typically evaluated by matching queries from one condition against a database from another condition. This tests the ability to recognize the same place when the query's condition differs from the database's condition. However, to map large environments, a database can be built from images collected by multiple robots or across multiple traversals under different conditions. In this setting, condition blindness---the ability to remain invariant to condition differences among database images---becomes important, but standard cross-condition evaluation does not provide a controlled assessment of this ability. Therefore, we introduce Distractor-Augmented Recall (DAR) to measure condition blindness in a controlled manner. Across eleven methods and six datasets, we find that differences in condition blindness can be larger than Recall@1 alone would suggest. To improve the condition blindness that DAR reveals, we compare three methods that make VPR descriptors more invariant to condition changes through post-processing. Among the three methods, we demonstrate INLP on a database built from multiple traversals under different conditions, showing that it can improve the performance of existing VPR methods.

papers.title: CS-PIKAN: Curvilinear Separable Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Autograd-Based Metric Evaluation and Certified Error Bounds for PDEs on Complex Domains
papers.abstract: Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (PIKANs) offer effective neural solvers for partial differential equations (PDEs), but their conventional formulations rely on Cartesian domains and scattered collocation points, often resulting in high computational costs, approximate boundary enforcement, and no rigorous error guarantees. We introduce CT-PIKAN, which maps curvilinear domains to the unit square and computes all geometric quantities, including those required by the Laplace-Beltrami operator, through automatic differentiation. Building on this transformation, Curvilinear Separable PIKAN (CS-PIKAN) represents solutions as rank-R sums of products of one-dimensional KANs with topology-adapted bases (Fourier for periodic and Chebyshev for bounded coordinates and time). A separable envelope and transfinite lift enforce boundary and initial conditions exactly, while a single sqrt{g}-weighted residual is minimized on a stratified tensor grid, reducing network cost from the product to the sum of grid sizes. We derive a metric-explicit Poincar'e constant, establish computable a-posteriori error bounds for elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic problems, and prove that the loss provides an unbiased estimator of the squared residual norm underlying these bounds. Nine benchmarks cover advection, Poisson, and heat conduction on Cartesian, polar, wavy, annular, star-shaped, and sampled-boundary domains. Across three seeds, CS-PIKAN reduces the relative L2 error of CT-PIKAN by factors of 7-126 at equal or lower training cost (up to 10 times faster), with all certified bounds satisfied. Ablations highlight the importance of exact periodicity and boundary constraints; KAN factors outperform MLPs for transport-dominated problems but not smooth elliptic ones. Nevertheless, classical body-fitted solvers remain substantially cheaper at comparable accuracy for these two-dimensional linear problems.

papers.title: Beyond Co-Movement: Locality by Exposures Enables a Joint Factor-Graph Framework for Portfolio Diversification
papers.abstract: Current portfolio construction methods are either agnostic to the effects of idiosyncratic shocks (standard factor models) or to the latent data structure driving systematic returns (recent graph-based approaches). This presents an opportunity to combine the complementary market aspects captured by the factor and graph domains, allowing asset allocations to operate directly on the underlying market structure, rather than on its observed co-movement or its finite-sample artefacts. In this work, we introduce the Mutually-INformed Graph-Locality and Exposures framework (MINGLE), which mutually regularises the factor and graph domains by redefining graph locality through systematic factor exposure profiles, rather than via observed co-movements. This is formalised through a unified Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) framework that jointly learns a latent factor representation and its induced graph topology directly from market returns. The resulting exposure-similarity graph aligns more closely with established economic sectors than conventional correlation-based graphs. Portfolios constructed from this representation are shown to consistently outperform their correlation-based counterparts across a range of volatility regimes and transaction cost levels. For rigour, paired statistical testing confirms that these gains stem from the reconciliation of the graph and factor domains.

papers.title: Beyond Routing Weights: Faithful Response-Level Interpretation of Mixture-of-Experts Reward Models via Contribution Contrast
papers.abstract: Reward models are central to learning from human preferences, yet identifying what drives their predictions remains challenging. Recent sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reward models seek to improve interpretability by routing prompts to specialized experts and characterizing experts through examples with high routing weights. However, routing weights only reveal which prompts an expert $\textit{receives}$, not how it $\textit{judges}$ responses, providing only a partial account of expert behavior. We therefore propose $\textbf{Co}$ntribution-$\textbf{Co}$ntrast ($\textbf{CoCo}$) response-level interpretation, which faithfully characterizes experts' roles using chosen-rejected response pairs with the largest contribution contrasts, jointly capturing routing and preference behavior. Across automatic and human evaluations, CoCo yields more coherent, faithful, and specialized interpretations than router-based, score-based, and sparse autoencoder-based alternatives while maintaining competitive reward modeling accuracy. Overall, we provide a controlled study of how different example-selection signals affect the interpretability of MoE reward models.

papers.title: The Nuclear Decision-Making Benchmark: Evaluating Frontier LLM Tendencies in Escalation, Proliferation, Non-Proliferation, and Arms Control Scenarios
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are entering defense and national-security workflows. Seven of the nine nuclear-armed states have committed to keeping humans in control of decisions to use nuclear weapons, but LLMs may still shape the assessments and options that reach decision-makers. Scrutinizing that influence calls for evidence about how these models behave on nuclear-policy questions. Such evidence should cover more than crisis escalation and should separate a model's tendencies from artifacts of a single phrasing, ordering, or run; evaluations to date have not focused on these questions. We introduce the Nuclear Decision-Making Benchmark (NDM Bench), a dataset and reproducible framework for testing how the choice of model and the design of a question shape LLMs' answers on nuclear policy. Its 151 scenarios, written by international relations experts, span four domains: nuclear escalation (76), arms control (25), non-proliferation (25), and proliferation (25). Each scenario can be posed with different states in the decision-maker's role and with added framing sentences. Eight frontier LLMs answered every prompt five times, about 380,000 responses in all. Results highlight that models' choices differ by model and domain, and that in escalation, how often they choose a nuclear threat or nuclear use depends on the state being advised and, for some models, the framing. However, agreement across identical runs is often low, with all five runs agreeing on only 43% of escalation prompts. We release the scenarios, the prompts with their answer orders, and the parsed responses, along with documentation of how they were built and recommended practices for evaluations where there is no correct answer to grade against.

papers.title: OmniEdit-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Instruction-based Video Editing
papers.abstract: Instruction-based video editing (IVE) offers diverse applications, yet evaluating editing models remains challenging. Existing benchmarks suffer from two key limitations: narrow task coverage inherited from image editing that overlooks video-specific dimensions, and metrics that inadequately capture instruction fidelity, allowing visually plausible but incorrect edits to receive high scores. To address these limitations, we introduce OmniEdit-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark covering spatial, temporal, audio, and reference-based editing. It distinguishes between explicit and implicit instructions and incorporates reasoning-based scenarios to reflect real-world editing requirements. We further propose an evaluation framework that assesses accuracy, preservation, realism, and consistency using both human judges and a state-of-the-art vision-language model (VLM). An accuracy-aware penalty mechanism conditions the other three scores on accuracy, prioritizing instruction fidelity and penalizing plausible but incorrect edits. Experiments on prominent open-source and commercial IVE models reveal substantial room for improvement. OmniEdit-Bench provides a structured testbed for identifying model limitations and advancing instruction-based video editing. Project page: https://omniedit-bench.github.io.

papers.title: Scrouting: Cost-Aware Routing of Coding Agents by Scouting the Repository First
papers.abstract: Frontier language models can resolve repository-level software issues, but each attempt is expensive, and existing routers select a model from the issue text alone. We present SuperScout, which routes after scouting the repository: a 7B searcher, SuperScout-7B, first explores the repository and produces a structured handoff whose reproduction claims are sandbox-verified, with false claims stripped before delivery. The searcher's hidden states, together with the task text, then feed a resume-based router that dispatches the task to one of four frontier fixers. Adding a new fixer requires no retraining. On the full Python slice of SWE-bench Pro (266 tasks) under the benchmark's official capped budget tier, SuperScout matches the best single model's solve rate (159 of 266 for SuperScout, 158 for the best model) at about a fifth of the total cost per solve, and the reported configuration sits above the random traffic-splitting baseline. A no-router ablation, always the cheapest fixer with the handoff, ties the routed system on this benchmark, so the handoff rather than the routing decision carries the result. A paired calibration study points to the mechanism: the handoff appears to redistribute rather than add solving ability, lifting the three cheaper fixers while slightly hurting the strongest, though at $N=99$ the per-fixer effects are directional only; the searcher's hidden states improve cost routing on the calibration labels while the handoff's own text does not. The searcher's compute adds less than half a cent of GPU time per task.

papers.title: JUDOR: CTDE-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for the Co-Optimization of Joint UAV Motion and Decentralized Opportunistic Routing in Delay-Tolerant Network
papers.abstract: The growing deployment of delay-tolerant networks (DTNs) has made store-carry-forward (SCF) communication indispensable for operating under sparse intermittent connectivity. However, intermittent contact opportunities, finite node buffers, and limited message time-to-live (TTL) degrade message delivery performance and induce network congestion. Yet unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), with extended radio coverage and controllable trajectories, can bridge ground-node pairs that would otherwise suffer poor connectivity. Nevertheless, conventional routing schemes decouple UAV motion control from message replication, and consequently fail to leverage UAV mobility to proactively create future contact opportunities. This paper presents JUDOR (Joint-UAV-Decentralized-Opportunistic-Routing), a centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE)-based multi-agent reinforcement learning framework optimized for joint discrete UAV heading control and decentralized opportunistic routing. Specifically, we model the tightly coupled UAV motion-routing co-optimization task as a factored partially observable Markov decision process with a shared team reward. JUDOR adopts decentralized actors for local-node execution and a centralized critic used exclusively in training, with optional multi-horizon congestion-hotspot auxiliary supervision. Through evaluation across four distinct traffic modes, JUDOR yields consistent performance gains over both classical and learning-based DTN baselines, including PRoPHET and MaxProp, whilst preserving contact-limited decentralized execution suitable for real-world DTN deployments.

papers.title: From Multimessenger Inference to Simulations: A Ranked Ensemble of Finite-Temperature Equations of State
papers.abstract: We construct a set of microphysical, finite-temperature equations of state (EOSs) for numerical simulations of neutron star mergers and core-collapse supernovae that is consistent with modern constraints from nuclear theory and multimessenger astronomy and systematically spans the posterior distribution of allowed EOSs. The EOSs are based on a simplified Skyrme functional whose inputs are nuclear matter saturation properties, extended to supra-saturation densities through the speed of sound at a set of reference densities. The models are assigned continuous likelihood weights from chiral effective field theory and perturbative quantum chromodynamics calculations, the gravitational-wave signal GW170817, and four NICER mass-radius measurements. From the resulting catalog of 3.6 million EOSs, the posterior yields $R_{1.4} = 11.8^{+0.8}_{-0.7}$ km, $\Lambda_{1.4} = 342^{+181}_{-118}$, and $M_{\rm max}^{\rm TOV} = 2.17^{+0.23}_{-0.16}\,M_\odot$ (medians with 90% credible intervals). From this posterior we select a ranked twelve-member ensemble, headed by a fiducial, central EOS, whose members are individually plausible while bracketing the posterior spread of each neutron-star observable. For all ensemble members we generate general-purpose finite-temperature tables with the SROEOS code, each accompanied by nucleon effective-mass variants for systematic studies of thermal effects, to be made publicly available upon publication.

papers.title: Graph-of-Thoughts for LLM Causal Discovery with a Fairness-Pathway Case Study
papers.abstract: Methods that use large language models (LLMs) for causal discovery reason locally, deciding one variable pair or one node at a time, so they never compare alternative whole graphs. We introduce GoT-CD, a Graph-of-Thoughts method that asks an LLM for several complete candidate graphs from variable metadata alone, ranks them with a deterministic validity score, merges them under a hard union constraint, refines the merge, and projects the result to a DAG. We evaluate on Asia, Child, and an Alzheimer's disease graph with 100 samples and GPT-4o-mini. Over five seeds on Alzheimer's and Child, GoT-CD gives the highest mean F1 score and the lowest mean structural Hamming distance of the LLM methods, with 95% intervals of the difference excluding zero in seven of eight comparisons, and it returns a DAG in every run while using three LLM requests per graph. Replaying the logged runs without individual components attributes most of the gain to generating and merging several complete candidates. A case study on the effect of Sex on MOCA Score in the Alzheimer's graph shows the limits of structural scores: the fairness verdict drawn from the discovered graph disagrees with the reference verdict in twelve of fifteen LLM runs, including all five GoT-CD runs, which mostly drop the edge out of Sex. Graphs meant for a specific downstream analysis should therefore also be checked on the pathways that analysis depends on.

papers.title: Localize, Don't Beautify: Client-Side Control of Image-Editing APIs for Cosmetic Surgery Previews
papers.abstract: Ask a commercial image editor to preview a cosmetic procedure and it will often change more of the face than the request names: a jawline edit can also smooth the forehead or alter the eyes. Existing methods for confining an edit to one region require access to the model's internals, which a public editing API does not expose. We ask how much control is possible from the client side alone. In a pilot benchmark, five current commercial editing configurations perform facelift-style jaw-neck and rhinoplasty edits on synthetic faces under two levels of client-side control: the prompt alone, and a masked composite that cuts the edited region out of the response and pastes it back onto the original photograph through a landmark-derived mask. Of 162 attempted edits, 151 could be scored. ArcFace cosine measures identity preservation; a CIELAB pixel-change ratio measures how much change lands inside the requested region rather than a protected facial zone. On 15 faces, the masked composite improved localization over the paired prompt-only output by a median of 0.315 (95% face-clustered bootstrap interval 0.279-0.366) while retaining most of the target-region change. Editors differed in edit strength and identity retention, and one returned near-copies for the facelift request. This is a study of control, not clinical accuracy: the faces are synthetic, no surgeons rated the outputs, and each condition was generated once. Within that scope, keeping a surgical preview inside its intended region needs no access to the model; a mask and composite on the client enforce it across every editor tested, at low provider cost.

papers.title: Two-Parameter Ansatz for the Violation of Eigenstate Thermalization
papers.abstract: The eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) provides the prevailing framework for understanding quantum thermalization and ergodicity in isolated many-body systems. Yet, no general theory describes the continuous onset of ETH violation between the conventional ETH and its complete breakdown. Here, we introduce a two-parameter ansatz for ETH violation that unifies and distinguishes two mechanisms: fading ergodicity and trapped ergodicity. While fading ergodicity captures the established route to ergodicity breaking, trapped ergodicity describes a distinct scenario in which ETH is violated in finite systems but restored in the thermodynamic limit. We test this framework in the spin-1/2 $J_1$-$J_2$ chains with onsite disorder and a linear potential. In both cases, we find that the observed ETH violation is consistent with trapped ergodicity.

papers.title: MANGO-Grasp: Mahalanobis Fields over Geometry-Oriented 3D Gaussians for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasping
papers.abstract: Cross-embodiment dexterous grasping aims to synthesize stable grasps across heterogeneous multi-fingered hands with little or no embodiment-specific tuning. Existing interaction-centric methods achieve promising results, but their object representations often underrepresent local surface geometry, hand descriptors do not explicitly capture both morphology and kinematics, and hand-object interaction modeling is typically isotropic. We propose MANGO-Grasp, an anisotropic interaction framework that represents objects as geometry-oriented 3D Gaussian primitives to better preserve local surface geometry, and encodes hands into pretrained descriptors that capture both morphology and kinematics. Hand-object interaction is modeled using anisotropic Mahalanobis fields that reflect the directional nature of contact and guide a shared optimization for grasp realization across embodiments. On the CMAP and MultiGripperGrasp benchmarks, MANGO-Grasp outperforms the strongest seen-hand baseline by up to 8.24 percentage points in simulation. It also transfers zero-shot to the unseen SharpaWave hand, improving over the strongest zero-shot baseline by up to 16.57 percentage points, and achieves 86% success in real-world experiments. The code and additional materials are available at https://connor-zh.github.io/MANGO-Grasp/.

papers.title: CoNav-UAV: Cooperative Dual-Altitude Aerial Navigation via Stackelberg Learning
papers.abstract: Aerial search missions often require an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to locate a target from only a brief description of its appearance and surroundings, a task known as target-oriented aerial vision-and-language navigation (VLN). The task demands city-scale exploration and grounding as well as collision-free close-range approach, two interleaved processes that are difficult to reconcile within a single agent. Most existing methods adapt the ground VLN paradigm to a single UAV and rely on external assistance to compensate for its inefficiency. A recent attempt deploys two UAVs at complementary altitudes but still depends on privileged sensing and trains the two agents independently, precluding any mutual adaptation. We propose CoNav-UAV, which models the task as a Stackelberg game between a high-altitude leader and a low-altitude follower to capture their sequential decisions and asymmetric observations and utilities, with both agents using only onboard sensing. We introduce Iterative Stackelberg Learning, which tailors optimization to each agent's role: the leader's high-level vision-language reasoning builds on pretrained capabilities and is refined through memory-based in-context learning, while the follower's precise motion control is fine-tuned through DAgger-style expert distillation. Alternating the two updates lets each agent continually adapt to the other's evolving behavior. CoNav-UAV outperforms single- and dual-agent baselines across three high-fidelity urban scenes from the AerialVLN benchmark. It improves success rate by up to 30.8 points on the learning scene and by up to 9.0 points under cross-scene transfer, where the leader reuses its learned memory and the follower is adapted with 2.6-3.7 times less target-scene data. Extensive ablations confirm the contributions of key components and the benefit of mutual adaptation, with consistent gains across VLM backbones.

papers.title: Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation
papers.abstract: Emerging accelerators rarely ship with mature compiler backends, so recent work asks LLM agents to write native kernels directly from ISA documentation and simulator feedback. On two such accelerators, this direct workflow returns a correct kernel on only 17 of 38 workload instances, and most of its inference budget is spent re-deriving machine semantics and repairing illegal code rather than optimizing the workload. We present Contour, which consists of two parts. Contour-Explore replaces native-code generation with search over a mapping surface: a typed set of scheduling knobs and their legal domains, generated automatically from the accelerator's ISA description and the workload graph. A compiler-owned resolver completes partial assignments into legal plans and emits native code, so every evaluated candidate is verified against the compiler's default, and any policy can drive the search, including hill climbing, evolutionary search, and LLM agents. Compared with KernelCraft, a state-of-the-art agentic kernel generator, an LLM agent through Contour-Explore returns a verified kernel on every Gemmini and PLENA instance, produces 2.86x and 1.13x faster kernels on the instances where both succeed, and uses 26.3% and 83.4% fewer tokens per verified kernel. Contour-Ext extends the surface when search stalls: an LLM agent implements a new knob and its lowering in the compiler backend, and Contour-Ext accepts the extension only if the default path is byte-identical, every new value is numerically correct and changes the program, and the enlarged surface yields a measured gain. On VTA, Contour-Ext extends the AutoTVM surface of TVM, and AutoTVM's XGBTuner then finds 4.14x faster kernels; on PLENA, the extended surface makes the kernels found by hill climbing 1.20x faster.

papers.title: CADENA: Stepwise CAD Reverse Engineering
papers.abstract: Computer-Aided Design (CAD) underpins modern engineering, yet converting existing shapes into editable models still demands substantial expert effort. Most AI systems emit the entire CAD program in a single pass, never inspecting the intermediate geometry. In contrast, human engineers build a part feature by feature, checking after each operation what remains to be modeled. We introduce CADENA (Spanish for "chain"), a model that reconstructs a 3D mesh as a parametric CAD program, growing its sequence of operations one at a time and comparing the target with the currently predicted geometry at every step. We also address the lack of benchmarks for evaluating reverse-engineering methods on mechanical parts, introducing CADENA-Bench, a benchmark that measures performance across categories of mechanical parts. CADENA outperforms prior methods on CADENA-Bench and on the DeepCAD, Fusion 360, and MCB datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/zhemdi/cadena, model weights at https://huggingface.co/kulibinai/cadena, and CADENA-Bench at https://huggingface.co/datasets/kulibinai/cadena-bench.

papers.title: Compact SAT and MaxSAT Encodings for Business-to-Business Meeting Scheduling with Idle-Time Balancing
papers.abstract: Business-to-business meeting scheduling assigns pairwise meetings to slots and locations under availability, capacity, conflict, and precedence constraints. The published Boolean formulation retains removable assignments and uses pairwise precedence clauses. We combine solution-preserving domain filtering, sparse shared-suffix precedence encoding, and an objective minimizing the range of participants' internal idle-slot totals. Experiments on 126 official and 100 higher-density derived instances separate domain filtering, precedence representation, transitive relations, and optimization method. Under the same objective, the compact model achieves median paired reductions of 40.3% in clauses and 55.9% in peak memory relative to an adapted published MaxSAT formulation. Domain filtering alone reduces assignment variables by 24.1% and clauses by 16.2%. Suffix sharing gives an additional clause reduction of 0.5%-1.0% on official precedence instances, reaching 5.5% at the highest density in derived instances that retain a known feasible schedule. Total-time changes are small and mixed. Internal idle distinguishes short interruptions from longer waits; aggregate idle complements the range. In the original one-run comparison, all three SAT and MaxSAT methods solve every official instance with lower median total times than Gurobi.

papers.title: Low-lying singly heavy baryon states based on the rigorous calculation with the relativized quark model
papers.abstract: In this work, the low-lying $\mathbf{6}_{F}$ singly heavy baryon states with positive-parity are studied in detail in the framework of the relativized quark model by using the improved calculation scheme which has nicely explained the fine structure of the low-lying negative-parity singly heavy baryons. The low-lying spectra of all the singly heavy baryon families obtained in the same framework and calculation scheme are systematically analyzed. The baryon states marked with (mass)$J^{P}$ are obtained by considering the mixing effect rigorously. It is found that the mixing effect in the singly heavy baryons depends on the flavor symmetry of the two light quarks and the baryon parity. The results show that the high-precision calculation reproduces the majority of the assigned experimental masses within the maximum deviation range of 20 MeV and the mean absolute deviation between the calculated masses and the experimental data is only 6.88 MeV. The rigorous calculation achieved by the two-step GEM enables us to analyze the detailed behavior of the various strong interaction components within the baryons with a high-precision. The large amount of data obtained in this work serves as the useful references for related experimental and theoretical researches.

papers.title: Delayed Formation of Landau Polaritons in Phase-Resolved THz Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Strong light-matter coupling gives rise to polaritons through coherent and periodic energy exchange between electromagnetic cavity fields and material excitations. While this interaction is typically inferred from spectral mode splitting, its dynamics remain largely unexplored. Here, using phase-resolved terahertz time-domain spectroscopy, we observe vacuum Rabi oscillations of Landau polaritons formed by coupling the cyclotron resonance in a GaAs/AlGaAs two-dimensional electron gas with Fabry-Perot cavity modes. By employing cross-polarized spectroscopy and magnetic-field differential, we resolve the temporal beating of the cyclotron resonance oscillations. Supported by a quantum electrodynamic model, we show that the vacuum Rabi oscillations start after a delay corresponding to one cavity round-trip time. This demonstrates that the strong coupling regime sets up only after the formation of the cavity mode field. Our results provide direct insight into the dynamics of hybrid light-matter states in the THz regime.

papers.title: QAdapt: Noise-Adaptive Neural Pre-Decoding for Surface-Code Quantum Error Correction
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing relies on quantum error correction to protect logical information, requiring classical decoders that keep pace with syndrome generation. Heterogeneous, changing hardware noise and the distribution shift from simulation to experiment challenge the accuracy and robustness of fixed neural decoders. We present QAdapt, a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction. QAdapt learns local spatiotemporal correlations, continually adapts across noise environments, and passes the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder. Online elastic weight consolidation limits forgetting as training moves between measurement, idle, CNOT, and Pauli-bias noise regimes. At distance nine, the HTNet pre-decoder reduces equivalent per-round logical error by 15.64% relative to Ising-Fast, with 28.75% fewer parameters and 9.07% less matching-backend time. Online EWC reduces average forgetting by 76.52% relative to sequential fine-tuning. With weights frozen, it reduces equivalent per-round logical error by 5.66% relative to continued base-environment training on a fixed valid domain of 331 unseen compound-noise conditions; whole-sequence failure probability falls by 2.54% over all 396 conditions. On native Willow records, the corresponding per-round reductions are 19.44%, 17.47%, and 17.95% at 10, 30, and 50 rounds, without target-domain fine-tuning. These results show how adaptive neural pre-decoding can improve logical accuracy, preserve performance across noise regimes, and reduce residual matching workload within an established decoding pipeline.

papers.title: VETO: Towards Protecting Images From Frontier AI Editing
papers.abstract: Modern image editors blur the boundary between image editing and text-to-image synthesis, extracting people and objects from a single photo and inserting them into new scenes without subject-specific fine-tuning. Existing defenses struggle to disrupt such manipulations in these models without large, visibly damaging perturbations to the images. We introduce VETO, a white-box image-cloaking method for open-weight editors that maximizes the entropy of attention between reference image and generation tokens to disrupt selective retrieval of source details, while requiring neither the future editing instruction nor modifications to the model. We also introduce VetoBench, a benchmark of 300 benign and harmful tasks balanced between within-scene editing and recontextualization. Full Pareto evaluations on FLUX.2 and FIBO-Edit across three benchmarks and five perturbation budgets demonstrate overall better protection-fidelity trade-offs, particularly against recontextualization. Protected images remain effective on fine-tuned and distilled variants of the editor without reoptimization.

papers.title: SciFigQual-Bench: Scientific Figure Quality Assessment with Manuscript-Linked Context
papers.abstract: Scientific figure quality is bound to the manuscript: a crop can be visually clear and still contradict its caption or the paragraph that cites it. Most image quality assessment and chart-understanding methods target a detached visual surface or a question-answering score, rather than alignment among the figure, its caption, and the citing text. A single end-to-end prompt that sees the image and the text together still mixes what is visible with what the caption and the citing paragraph claim, so fluent wording can raise a visual score and missing text can be treated as low quality. To address this gap, we introduce SciFigQual-Bench, a manuscript-linked benchmark for published CS-conference figures that binds each figure to its caption and to index-resolved citing paragraphs, and scores visual clarity, layout, caption consistency, context consistency, and misleading risk, leaving a dimension unevaluated when its evidence is absent. SFQ-Agent reads the image and the text in separate calls and records modality-specific evidence. A cross-modal judge scores caption and citing-text alignment from those reports, and a deterministic runner keeps the visual scores, sets misleading risk by a fixed rule, and applies the written caps, so each dimension follows the rubric instead of a single end-to-end prompt. Experiments comparing this staged judge with single-pass and OCR-sidecar protocols find the closest point-estimate fit to mean human ratings under staged judging, while the gap between protocols remains small. Caption consistency remains the main gap, and agreement with the rater mean answers a different question from agreement among human raters. Project page: https://frankdengai.github.io/SciFigQual-Bench/

papers.title: The Best of Times, the Worst of Times: Moment-Based Analysis of Probabilistic Cost Structures
papers.abstract: Many practical costs---such as the completion time of a quantum repeater, the rounds of an RFID collision-resolution protocol, or the response time of a fork--join computation---are described by hierarchical cost expressions: a tree of independent subcomputations with nonnegative integer costs, combined by addition, max, and min. We compute their moments with sound error bounds. Moment-based analyses for additive costs do not apply, because the moments of $\max(X,Y)$ are not determined by those of $X$ and $Y$; propagating full distributions becomes expensive as trees grow; and scalable approximations are hand-derived for specific structures and lack error bounds. Our analysis proceeds bottom-up, summarizing each subtree by a surrogate distribution: an exact short-horizon prefix plus a compact parametric tail fitted to preserve the queried moment. Each prefix is computed exactly from the children's prefixes---for a retry, whose cost sums an unbounded number of attempts, by solving a local recurrence equation---so all approximation is confined to the tails. Abstraction introduces shape error but no moment error; nonlinear operators, such as max and min, convert shape error into moment error. The analysis tracks two bounds, one on shape error and one on moment error. Tracking both lets it report a sound interval for the mean, the second moment, and the variance. Lengthening the prefix, or solving subtrees exactly, narrows the interval at the cost of additional computation. For quantum-repeater chains of up to 4096 links with high swap-success probability, our Dickens tool bounds the mean completion time within 1%, whereas the exact Markov-chain solution exhausts memory with 16 links, and the best hand-derived approximation we evaluated has 47% error with 64 links. Dickens also bounds second moments, variances, and deadline-miss probabilities, and handles RFID and fork--join costs.

papers.title: Data-driven impeller model for efficient large eddy simulations of metastable von K\'arm\'an flows
papers.abstract: The von K\'arm\'an turbulent swirling flow exhibits intriguing large-scale metastable dynamics, including low-frequency state switching. The study of state switching demands long-duration high-fidelity simulations at high Reynolds numbers that capture the flow generated by the impellers. Blade-resolved Large Eddy Simulations (LES) are computationally prohibitive, limiting access to these slow dynamics. Here, we develop a model for the action of the impellers on the flow using experimental data from Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and torque measurements of the von K\'arm\'an flow. The impeller-region velocity is parametrized via B-splines and coupled to the LES through momentum forcing. An initial set of B-spline coefficients is inferred using the Optimizing a DIscrete Loss (ODIL) framework constrained by the Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations, PIV measurements in the optically accessible portion of the device, and impeller torque measurements. The coefficients are then refined by the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), which minimizes the discrepancy between the LES time-averaged velocity and torque and their experimental counterparts. Using the data-driven impeller model, we perform long-duration LES of the von K\'arm\'an flow. We find that the simulation reproduces the mean flow in the bulk and displays metastable state-switching dynamics. We further show that these metastable states are not axisymmetric and consist of an alternating four-cell flow pattern that slowly rotates around the axis of the cylindrical vessel. The proposed approach provides a practical and computationally efficient route to investigating large-scale dynamics in impeller-driven turbulent flows.

papers.title: Making Mathematical Knowledge Explainable, Accessible and Interoperable Through Large Language Model Integration
papers.abstract: Mathematical models are central to formalizing research problems, yet their documentation often falls short of FAIR principles. Knowledge bases such as the Mathematical Model Database (MathModDB) address this gap by providing curated, semantically rich representations of mathematical models. Built on Wikibase, the same open-source infrastructure underlying Wikidata, MathModDB utilizes Semantic Web technologies to support Linked Open Data, collaborative editing, and the storage of semantically enriched metadata, making it a domain-specific knowledge graph within the broader Wikidata ecosystem. However, access to MathModDB currently requires either navigating a complex web interface or proficiency in SPARQL and Wikibase APIs, posing significant barriers for potential users. In addition, the combination of such curated knowledge bases with actual research data stored, e.g., in Dataverse repository instances, remains a challenge. To overcome these limitations, we propose integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with MathModDB via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes a vector-indexed schema retrieval and Steiner-tree-based join planner, combining dialogue-based natural language interaction with curated, epistemically grounded knowledge. Although instantiated on MathModDB, the architecture can be applied to other Wikibase-based systems. We demonstrate that this approach enables epistemically grounded LLM usage, improves model explainability and accessibility beyond what the standard Wikibase interface offers, and simplifies interoperability with external databases and tools, such as Dataverse data repositories. We illustrate the benefits of combining the accessibility of an LLM with the epistemic safety of a curated knowledge base through the adaptability of the MCP protocol by two use cases.

papers.title: Precise cover times for branching random walks on Hamming graphs: (iterated) logarithmic corrections
papers.abstract: We prove tight asymptotics of the cover time $\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}(d)$ of a continuous-time branching random walk on the Hamming graph $\{0,1,\dots,b-1\}^d$, as $d\to\infty$. We focus on the slow-branching regime, where particles move at rate one and branch at rate $\lambda\in(0,1)$. For $b>2$, we show that $\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}(d)=x_\star d+\lambda^{-1}\log d+O_{\mathbb P}(1)$. For $b=2$, we show that $\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}(d)=x_\star d+\chi^{-1}\log\log d+O_{\mathbb P}(1)$. Here, $x_\star$ and $\chi$ are explicit positive constants depending only on $b$ and $\lambda$. Our results sharpen previously known linear-order estimates. The dichotomy reflects the geometry of the last uncovered region: for $b>2$, there are exponentially many antipodes, whereas the binary hypercube has a unique antipode and its neighbors govern the final coverage. Our proofs combine classic spine change of measure techniques and many-to-few estimates with a multiscale decomposition of the genealogy and a weighted martingale analysis of the early population.

papers.title: Where Is the Cost of Third-Party API Routers in Agentic Software Development?
papers.abstract: Third-party API routers have become a common layer that unifies access across increasingly diverse LLM providers. In coding-agent workflows, high-autonomy operation is widely adopted because it reduces interaction overhead. As a result, a third-party API router, which sits between the agent and the upstream provider, inevitably occupies the trusted path. It can inspect and modify every request and response, yet no mechanism verifies alignment between the provider's output and the repository-level actions ultimately executed by the agent. Consequently, client-side permission mechanisms may become ineffective in practice. Whether this control gap produces real, hard-to-detect effects on software development tasks remains empirically unmeasured. In this paper, we conduct an empirical study of router-side injection in coding agents, examining four intervention levels of increasing subtlety: Response Substitution (L1), Response Append (L2), LLM-Polished Injection (L3), and LLM-Polished with Distribution Alignment Injection (L4). Moreover, we develop SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, with a curated dataset of 400 samples. We evaluate four representative coding agents, and further evaluate whitelist-based execution control and LLM review. Router-side intervention substantially alters repository-level actions and remains difficult for existing client-side safeguards to detect. Without additional mitigations, all evaluated agents achieved a defense success rate of 0 percent across all injection levels. Client-side mitigations and reactive reviews improve resistance but do not fully restore end-to-end control, motivating provider-side output-integrity guarantees. Our code is available at https://github.com/Riyasushin/SIDEL.

papers.title: Nahm Sums Dual to Zagier's Rank Three Examples and Related Identities
papers.abstract: In 2007, Zagier identified twelve families of candidates for rank three modular Nahm sums and established the modularity of three of them. The remaining cases were subsequently confirmed by Wang. Zagier's duality observation indicates that the Nahm sums associated with the duals of these examples might still be modular. We confirm that this is indeed true. The modularity of the dual of the sixth example was previously established by Milas and Wang, while that of the dual of the eleventh example was partially established by Shi and Wang. We settle all remaining cases, thereby establishing the modularity of every defined dual in Zagier's rank three list. We achieve this by proving new Rogers--Ramanujan type identities that express the relevant Nahm sums as finite sums of infinite products. Along the way we discover two new families of modular rank three Nahm sums. As applications, we prove some Nahm sum identities conjectured by Cao--Wang, Shi--Wang and Li.

papers.title: From the Early Slope to Curvature: Future Prospects and challenges for Astrophysical Parameter Estimation Using the Core-Collapse Supernova High-Frequency Feature
papers.abstract: Gravitational-wave (GW) signals from core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) contain both stochastic and deterministic components. Among these, the High-Frequency Feature (HFF), associated with Proto-Neutron Star (PNS) oscillations, has emerged as an observable for probing dense-matter physics. Previous studies of the HFF have primarily focused on its early-time slope as a diagnostic of PNS contraction and its dependence on the nuclear equation of state (EOS). In this work, we investigate recovering higher-order features of the HFF evolution, such as its curvature, from core-collapse supernova numerical simulations. By analyzing 2D and 3D waveforms injected into real interferometric noise, we apply the coherent WaveBurst algorithm in its cWB-XP implementation to reconstruct the HFF of recovered events. Comparing reconstructions at different signal strengths allows us to examine the extent to which the HFF remains accessible beyond its early linear evolution

papers.title: MOLT: A Hugging Face-Native, Minimal, and Scalable Framework for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) research iterates quickly on agents, rewards, and learning algorithms, while policies have grown to hundreds of billions of parameters and beyond. Existing open frameworks force a choice: those that are easy to modify do not scale to the largest models, and those that scale rely on Megatron, which needs dedicated bridge code for every model family and several times more framework code. We present MOLT, an open-source framework built for research that is Hugging Face-native, minimal, and scalable. Its code is easy to modify: the entire RL path is approximately 9.2K lines of Python with one training backend and one rollout engine, so a researcher or an AI coding agent can read it in full and edit the code that actually runs. A Hugging Face checkpoint is loaded directly into a PyTorch FSDP2 trainer with tensor, expert, and context parallelism, so a new model family needs no bridge, and the same code scales from a 4B model to a 753B one. Existing OpenAI- and Anthropic-SDK agents are trained by redirecting their client, with automatic handling of agents that rewrite their own context; training is fully asynchronous; and trajectory data stay in a distributed object store. With MOLT, a 30B mixture-of-experts tool agent trains stably for 1,464 asynchronous updates, a visual computer-use agent improves on OSWorld, asynchronous training is 2.40 times faster than synchronous training, and pipeline throughput reaches 92% of a Megatron-based stack. Its trainer, NeMo AutoModel, trains models of one to 2.8 trillion parameters.

papers.title: Transverse-momentum resummation effects on angular coefficients in Z and W boson hadroproduction
papers.abstract: We present a comprehensive analysis of the angular coefficients of $Z$ and $W$ boson production at hadron colliders in different kinematical ranges, using data from the ATLAS, LHCb, and CMS Collaborations at the LHC, including the recent CMS measurement at $\sqrt{s}=13$~TeV, as well as CDF data at the Tevatron. We provide theoretical predictions obtained by consistently combining the resummation of logarithmically enhanced QCD corrections at small transverse momentum $q_T$ up to next-to-next-to-leading logarithmic accuracy (NNLL) with the fixed-order calculation through $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_S^2)$. The fixed-order helicity cross sections entering the finite component are evaluated using the new complete analytic NLO calculation implemented in the DYTurbo program. This implementation makes it possible to obtain fast and numerically stable predictions for all the angular coefficients and to perform an extensive study of their theoretical uncertainties. We quantify the impact of transverse-momentum resummation on the angular coefficients and we estimate the associated theoretical uncertainties, including scale variations, parton distribution functions, non-perturbative effects, the treatment of the transition region and the recoil prescription used to generate the lepton angular distribution of the resummed component. Within the estimated theoretical uncertainties, resummation improves the description of several measurements, particularly for $A_2$, while its impact on $A_0$ depends more strongly on the dataset and on the theoretical choices. The Lam--Tung combination $A_0-A_2$ is essentially unaffected by resummation.

papers.title: Colloquium: Semi-Dirac Fermions in Quantum Matter
papers.abstract: This article reviews the recent progress on the subject of semi-Dirac fermions, two dimensional quasiparticles that disperse quadratically, as Galilean invariant particles, or linearly, as massless relativistic particles, depending on their direction of motion. These quasiparticles exist at phase boundaries set by the continuous change in the connectivity of Fermi surfaces, known as Lifshitz transitions. The basic properties and the current experimental evidence of the existence of these quasiparticles in both synthetic lattices and quantum materials are presented. The many-body problem of semi-Dirac fermions is discussed from a theoretical perspective with an eye to physical observables of relevance to experiments.

papers.title: UniRank: Benchmarking Ranking Models for Unified Sequential Modeling and Feature Interaction
papers.abstract: Ranking is a core stage in online advertising and recommender systems. Modern ranking models increasingly unify sequential modeling and feature interaction, yet many advances rely on proprietary data, closed implementations, and large-scale industrial infrastructure. This setting limits reproducible comparison and hinders academic study of scaling laws, long-sequence modeling, and multi-task ranking. To address these limitations, this paper proposes UniRank, an open benchmark for ranking models that unify sequential modeling and feature interaction. UniRank uses chronological pointwise autoregressive supervision, standardizes evaluation across feedback tasks, and provides a PyTorch toolkit with Distributed Data Parallel training, operator optimization, mixed-precision training, attention optimization, and other efficiency techniques that reduce hardware requirements. We benchmark 15 representative unified ranking models on five public datasets from short-video, advertising, and e-commerce platforms, with the largest containing over 700 million instances and the longest behavior sequence exceeding $10^5$ interactions. UniRank provides a reproducible foundation for comparing unified ranking models, studying scaling laws under limited compute, and narrowing the gap between academic and industrial ranking research. We believe UniRank benefits researchers, practitioners, and beginners through reproducible experiments, production-oriented evaluation, and accessible implementations. Code and data are available at https://github.com/salmon1802/UniRank.

papers.title: Quantum Circuits for Quantum Spatial Search on $d$-Dimensional Hypercubic Lattices
papers.abstract: We propose an explicit quantum-circuit construction for quantum spatial search based on discrete-time quantum walks on $d$-dimensional hypercubic lattices and systematically evaluate its circuit-resource scaling. Although the algorithmic performance of quantum spatial search has been extensively studied, a systematic evaluation of its circuit-resource scaling remains limited. We implement the flip-flop shift operator using coin-controlled modular increment and decrement operations for position updates and a single $X$ gate for direction reversal. We compare four implementations of the position update based on the quantum Fourier transform (QFT), ripple-carry addition, multi-controlled $X$ (MCX) gates, and automatically synthesized arithmetic. The results show that the QFT-based implementation reduces circuit width and depth, while the ripple-carry implementation reduces the CX-gate count at the cost of additional ancilla qubits. We also extend the construction to non-periodic boundary conditions by introducing self-loops at lattice boundaries. We confirm that numerical simulations of the circuits reproduce the theoretical search dynamics for $d=2,3,4$, and $5$ under periodic boundary conditions and for $d=2$ under non-periodic boundary conditions. For $N=L^d$ lattice sites, the circuit width scales as $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$. We derive asymptotic upper bounds on the total circuit depth of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N}\log^{5/2} N)$ for $d=2$ and $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N}\log^2 N)$ for $d\geq3$, consistent with the numerical results. Furthermore, CX-gate depolarizing noise simulations show that reducing the CX-gate count improves noise robustness. These results provide guidance for efficient quantum-circuit design for spatial search on hypercubic lattices.

papers.title: Operational Proto-Introspection in Looped Language Models: Reading Correctness Before the Answer
papers.abstract: Can one tell, while a language model reasons, whether its answer will be right? Looped models are a good place to ask: they run the same layers several times per token, leaving one hidden state per loop for a probe to read. I probe Ouro-RLTT, a 2.6B-parameter looped model, for what these states reveal about how its reasoning will end. I call such information operational proto-introspection: operational because it is defined by what a probe can read, and proto because nothing here shows that the model itself uses it. In part, yes. Reading the first 48 tokens of reasoning, from answers that state no answer yet, a probe on the hidden states reaches an AUROC of 0.758 on a synthetic logic task, against 0.515 for token confidence. Question difficulty is a rival explanation: on 1,164 further questions, token confidence plus simple features of the question predict about as well. It is not only difficulty: between two answers to the same question, the probe scores the correct one higher 74% of the time. A fine-tuned language model reading the same tokens does about as well. On GSM8K and on a second checkpoint this within-question test is unresolved. A probe that ranks finished candidate answers is weak at layer 8 on the first loop, much better on the second, and as accurate as the last layers by the third, on four Ouro checkpoints. The direction it reads is largely shared across loops: a probe trained on the last loop reads the first nearly as well as a probe trained there. The signal helps decide what to do with finished outputs. It improves abstention over surface features and picks correct answers among candidates better than chance, though surface features pick about as well. Once several samples are finished, a baseline that knows their agreement leaves the answer-free probe nothing measurable to add. None of my attempts to use it to make the model generate better answers worked.

papers.title: Distributed Topological Charge and Spinorial Holonomy in Yukawa-Regularized Graphene Disclinations
papers.abstract: Conical geometries provide the standard description of disclinations, but they concentrate the curvature at a singular apex. We introduce a Yukawa-type regularization that replaces this singularity by a smooth curvature distribution while preserving the asymptotic topology of the defect. Exact expressions are obtained for the conformal factor, curvature, and enclosed topological charge. The resulting geometry exhibits a scale-dependent topological charge and a corresponding radius-dependent holonomy, establishing a direct connection between distributed curvature and geometric phases. We further investigate the dynamics of massless Dirac quasiparticles in this background and show that the regularized core modifies the spin connection while preserving the asymptotic topological signature of the defect. These results provide a finite-core extension of the conventional conical description and offer a natural framework for studying geometric and topological effects in graphene-like systems.

papers.title: Particle accelerators as a path to intergovernmental collaboration: the case of the first electron positron collider and the power of theoretical physics
papers.abstract: I revisit the history of the first matter-antimatter collider built in Italy in 1960 and carried to success through an inter-European collaboration with France, to underline the need for large intergovernmental efforts in the realization of particle accelerators such as the proposed electron synchrotron in the Greater Caribbean region. The foundational role of the Austrian born theoretical physicist Bruno Touschek and his life path through Europe before and after World War II is briefly recalled. The role of CERN as a post-war intergovernmental institution in jump-starting the international collaboration between the Frascati National Laboratories in Italy and the Laboratoire de l'Accelerateur Lineaire d'Orsay in France is highlighted through historical documents, and contributions from interviews with the protagonists of Touschek's game-changing proposal.

papers.title: Relativistic bound-state solutions for a non-central Schi\"oberg-type hyperbolic potential with double ring-shaped angular terms
papers.abstract: Singular interactions can reshape quantum spectra by changing admissible wavefunction domains. In this study, we investigate this mechanism in the Klein--Gordon equation for a non-central Schi\"oberg-type hyperbolic potential with double ring-shaped angular barriers. Equal scalar and vector couplings separate the radial and angular dynamics. We solve the angular equation exactly on each hemisphere with principal boundary conditions and treat the radial equation with the Greene--Aldrich approximation, obtaining Jacobi-polynomial wavefunctions and an implicit relativistic quantization condition. With this boundary realization, the equatorial inverse-square singularity splits configuration space into reflection-related sectors with identical angular spectra. Reducing the barrier to zero while retaining the equatorial wall selects the odd-reflection spectral branch of the regular full-domain problem; a single hemisphere has no intrinsic parity.
