The nonrelativistic limit recovers the corresponding Schr\"odinger formulation. State-resolved nonrelativistic and relativistic benchmarks quantify the centrifugal error. In a dimensionless relativistic example, the relative error in the remaining binding exceeds unity near threshold although the absolute energy error decreases. For NaH and Na$_2$, low-lying central-radial vibrational energies agree reasonably with spectroscopic reference values, whereas the global radial shape limits near-dissociation accuracy and gives an incorrect NaH bound-state count.

papers.title: Efficient logical operations in quantum LDPC codes using simple resource states
papers.abstract: Quantum LDPC codes provide a substantial reduction in qubit overhead required for fault-tolerant quantum computation compared to surface code, thanks to their high encoding rate. However, operating simultaneously on multiple logical qubits encoded in the same block is more challenging and may slow down logical operations. Prior work addresses this problem by designing complex resource states to perform logical measurements in LDPC codes. Here, we propose an approach that only consumes cat states. Whereas previous work on cat-based measurements focuses on a single logical measurement, we design a protocol for the joint measurement of $\ell$ commuting logical operators. The key ingredient is the design of a scheduler code determining the measurement sequence and allowing for the decoding of all logical measurement outcomes. Numerical simulations with the LDPC codes Q70 and Q102 of the walking cat architecture show a reduction of nearly $3\times$ in the number of cat-based measurements required versus the Viterbi method for measuring $\ell=20$ commuting logical operators. Combining our logical measurement protocols with a new variant of the CliNR partial error correction scheme, we achieve a reduction of up to $73\times$ versus the Viterbi method for random Clifford circuits. Our approach also applies to non-Clifford gates, producing a reduction of up to $5\times$ versus the Viterbi method for Toffoli gates.

papers.title: Fast ungated five-dimensional cardiac MRI on a 1.5 T MR-linac for MRI-guided radiotherapy
papers.abstract: Background: Stereotactic arrhythmia radiotherapy (STAR) for patients with ventricular tachycardia is currently limited by complex cardiorespiratory motion. Current 5D-MRI motion models require long acquisition and reconstruction times, limiting clinical viability. Objective: To develop a fast, ungated 5D-MRI reconstruction method for personalized motion characterization to support MRI-guided STAR treatments. Methods: We propose a fast, ungated 5D-MRI reconstruction method based on the CMR-MOTUS framework. The method uses a 3D Cartesian acquisition with a joint optimization framework to reconstruct a motion-corrected reference image and low-rank deformation vector fields (DVFs). By exploiting the low rank structure, we explicitly disentangle respiratory and cardiac motion during optimization. Then, the DVFs are used for 5D-MRI reconstruction with a retrospectively adjustable number of motion states. Validation was performed using digital and physical cardiorespiratory phantoms. Furthermore, the approach was evaluated using 10 healthy volunteers, comparing motion consistency with 2D cine MRI. Results: Validation of 5D CMR-MOTUS using digital and physical phantoms demonstrated accurate 5D-MRI reconstruction. In the physical phantom, 5D CMR-MOTUS achieved a left-ventricle DICE of 0.96 +/- 0.01. In the volunteer cohort, the 5D-MRI scans showed strong motion to 2D cine MRI, with a cardiac motion error of 0.1 +/- 0.9 mm and a respiratory motion error of 0.2 +/- 2.9 mm. Crucially, 5D-MRI data were acquired in 1 minute and reconstructed in 6 minutes. Conclusions: The proposed 5D-MRI method enables rapid, high-quality, and personalized motion characterization, demonstrating potential for integration into MRI-guided STAR treatments. Data Availability: The 3D k-space data and 5D reconstructions for the ten volunteers are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21278894
authors: C. A. T. van den Berg

papers.title: A Performance Model for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Workflows
papers.abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical workflows are expected to underpin practical quantum computing, yet the community lacks a shared framework for reasoning about integration requirements. We introduce a runtime model that decomposes workflow execution into quantum compute, classical compute, and communication costs at two levels of analysis. At the application level, where communication overhead only affects performance, we use a communication-to-computation ratio to quantify its impact on runtime. At the real-time level, when communication overhead determines feasibility, we examine how decoding and feedback latency affect logical operation times and resource requirements. The model evaluates execution with allocated resources, excluding scheduling and resource management. Applied to representative workflows, it shows that the compute-intensive applications, including those requiring HPC resources, are largely insensitive to communication overhead. However, the model identifies when hardware evolution, such as faster quantum processing and greater parallelism, can shift this balance toward communication bottlenecks.

papers.title: Learning-Driven Channel Representation for Wireless Localization: From Channel Observations to Location Inference
papers.abstract: Wireless observations capture radio signal responses formed through interactions with propagation environments and spatial geometry. In integrated sensing and communication, such observations have become an important basis for high-accuracy localization beyond conventional channel estimation. Learning-driven methods learn implicit relations between channel propagation and spatial position, enabling location inference under complex channel conditions. However, the useful information is tightly coupled with spatial layout, environmental dynamics, and system configurations. This coupling obscures the inference process and weakens performance consistency across scenarios. In this paper, we review learning-driven high-accuracy localization techniques with channel representations as the organizing view. The survey covers typical channel observation forms and analyzes their physical meanings. We also review channel feature extraction and representation learning methods, and summarize methods according to the acquisition, organization, adaptation, and reuse of channel representations. Typical methods are compared in terms of accuracy, applicable conditions, data requirements, and generalization. We model the localization process as a unified ``wireless observation--channel representation--location inference'' framework and use information bottleneck theory to highlight that the quality and usability of channel representations are critical to exploiting propagation information and play a decisive role in localization performance. Finally, we summarize the key challenges in moving from experimental studies to real deployment and present our perspectives on these issues.

papers.title: Electrons Hopping across a Molecular Network: Spectra and Symmetries
papers.abstract: We investigate interacting spinless electrons on finite molecular networks described by a tight-binding Hubbard Hamiltonian. The interplay between network geometry, Coulomb interactions and discrete symmetries is analysed for rings with $L=3,4,5,6$ nodes, filled with one, two or three electrons. Special attention is devoted to the role of the network symmetries in determining the structure of the many-body spectrum and the Mulliken classification of the eigenstates. Using group-theoretical methods, we examine the evolution of the spectra in the presence of an external magnetic flux. The Zeeman effect lifts degeneracies and results in combination with the Coulomb interaction to avoided crossings in symmetry sectors. We identify a qualitatively distinction between systems with an even and odd number of particles. At half-filling, particle-hole symmetry (duality) protects selected symmetry sectors against Zeeman splitting.

papers.title: Disagreement-Guided Agentic Data Curation for Multimodal Safety
papers.abstract: Written safety policies in multimodal settings define categories whose visual boundaries span many contexts. We study disagreement as a signal for identifying useful synthetic boundary cases. Our pipeline generates policy-conditioned images, selects cases with target--rater or inter-rater disagreement, conditionally escalates unresolved cases, and retrieves the resulting rater-labeled examples as in-context demonstrations. On a failure-enriched multimodal safety benchmark, policy grounding reduces false negative rate (FNR) from 0.875 to 0.413 and raises F1 from 0.220 to 0.731; retrieval from 50 disagreement-selected examples further reduces FNR to 0.245, compared with 0.297 from a 350-example Regular pool. The selected memory also improves a different target-model family, with a smaller gain on a proprietary benchmark with a refined policy. In a blinded human study, experts disagree on 24% of disagreement-guided images and 17% of baseline-curated images. These findings support traceable, disagreement-guided curation for multimodal safety evaluation and example selection.

papers.title: A Geometric Coding Theorem
papers.abstract: This paper establishes a direct analogue of the classical Coding Theorem in the setting of symmetry groups. We consider computable bijections on the set of binary strings and define the symmetry prior of a string x as the probability that a randomly chosen symmetry from a given group G has x as its unique fixed point. We show that for any fix-retractable symmetry group G, a group admitting a computable section that selects an isolating symmetry for every string, the symmetry prior is a universal lower semi-computable semi-measure. In this case, the Geometric Coding Theorem holds. This result is a coding-theoretic restatement of a theorem of Trejo, Kreinovich and Longpr\'e, who showed that the complexity of describing a string by a symmetry with that string as its unique fixed point equals its Kolmogorov complexity. Our contribution is to recast it in terms of algorithmic probability and to treat the symmetry group as a parameter, identifying fix-retractability as exactly the condition under which symmetry complexity collapses onto Kolmogorov complexity.

papers.title: Meta-Learning Preferences for Multilingual LLM Alignment
papers.abstract: Unequal availability of human preference data across languages poses a significant challenge for aligning large language models in multilingual settings. To address the lack of sufficient data in low-resource language alignment, we propose a meta-learning framework for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Direct Preference Optimization. By leveraging preference data from other languages, our framework learns a transferable initialization that enables effective adaptation to a target language with minimal data. We provide theoretical guarantees for both the meta-reward modeling and meta-policy optimization settings, and empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on multilingual benchmarks. In an extremely low-resource setting with only 100 target-language preference samples, our approach achieves up to $33.4\%$ win-rate improvements over baseline methods, and consistently outperforms baselines across multiple target languages and model scales. Our approaches retain these advantages across different combinations of meta-training languages and varying linguistic distances from the target languages.

papers.title: Ascent and descent of operators concerning Jordan products
papers.abstract: Let $\mathcal B(\mathcal X)$ be the algebra of all bounded linear operators on a Banach space $\mathcal{X}$ over the real or complex field $\mathbb F$ with $\dim\mathcal X \ge 3$. In this paper, we give several properties of the ascent (descent) of operators or Jordan products of operators in $\mathcal B(\mathcal X)$ and use these properties to characterize certain operators such as algebraic operators, rank-one, rank-two operators, rank-one nilpotent operators as well as some relations between operators in terms of ascent (descent) of Jordan products. As an application, we give a characterization, up to a multiplier of nonlinear functional $f:\mathcal B(\mathcal X)\to \mathbb F^*$, of ring isomorphisms of $\mathcal B(\mathcal X)$ in the case $\dim \mathcal X=\infty$ and Jordan isomorphisms of $\mathcal B(\mathcal X)$ in the case $\dim \mathcal X<\infty$ via the maps with range containing all operators of rank at most three that preserve the ascent of Jordan products of operators. A slightly different characterization in term of descent is also obtained.

papers.title: Local statistics and average rank of genus $g$ hyperelliptic curves with a Weierstrass point
papers.abstract: In this paper, we determine the probability that a genus $g$ hyperelliptic curve with a Weierstrass point over a number field has good reduction at a given prime of residue characteristic $>2g+1$. We also obtain analogous probability formulas for several other reduction types, including cases with positive toric or unipotent rank. As an application, assuming the Hasse--Weil conjecture and the generalized Riemann hypothesis, we derive an explicit upper bound for the average analytic rank of genus $g$ hyperelliptic curves with a Weierstrass point.

papers.title: What Does a Temporal Benchmark Score Measure? Decomposing Channel Use in Video VLM Evaluation
papers.abstract: A score on a temporal video question answering benchmark is meant to measure that a model has temporal understanding, but it conflates two questions. (1)~is the question even temporal, does it need several frames and their order? And (2)~when it does, does the model recover the order from the pixels, or read it off the positional encoding (RoPE)? Most of a temporal score answers neither, since a single frame and answer priors often carry it, and the field's validity checks, frame-shuffle sensitivity and multi-frame gain, speak only to (1). For (2) we score a reversal conflict, frames reversed while RoPE stays forward, two ways: label-free, as the accuracy lost against the forward labels, and against reversed labels wherever labels transform deterministically under time reversal. This separates a model that follows the reversed content from one merely disrupted. The two readings dissociate two similarly scoring models at both model scales. Qwen3-VL answers the reversed event it actually sees, reading the visual sequence. Molmo2 correctly reports a backwards video when positions agree, and flipping only the RoPE indices flips its prediction to the forward events, i.e. it reads positions. We call these regimes \emph{visual-sequence-dominant} and \emph{position-dominant}. Controls show reversed content is processable whenever the channels agree, and that both families share a bias toward describing events as running forward (arrow-of-time prior) that, being similar in strength, cannot by itself account for the dissociation. The distinction matters because the two channels fail on opposite inputs: two models with the same score are not interchangeable.

papers.title: Bringing Back Rule Induction to Fluid Intelligence Research? An Initial Validation of the ARC-AGI Benchmark in Humans
papers.abstract: Two competing perspectives on fluid intelligence (gf) measures propose that performance is primarily constrained either by working memory capacity or by the ability to induce novel relations. The first perspective is currently dominant in measurement, as evident from the use of a limited set of recurring rules, whereas the second perspective is reflected in many definitions but rarely present in measurement. The ARC-AGI benchmark predominantly requires rule induction and was proposed as a measure of gf for both humans and artificial systems. However, its psychometric properties have not yet been examined in human samples. We therefore investigated the psychometric characteristics and nomological network of ARC-AGI in a first study with 100 participants. A compilation of ARC-AGI items showed good psychometric properties and correlated substantially with figural fluid intelligence as measured by a figural reasoning test ($\rho$ = .63). Associations with figural originality were weak. These findings provide initial support for the validity of ARC-AGI as a measure of human fluid intelligence. Future research should include more rule induction tasks as well as additional multivariate covariates. This study is unusual by studying a task in humans that was initially designed for machines. We suggest systematically embedding AI benchmarks into the nomological network of human cognitive abilities to enable more systematic evaluation and interdisciplinary cooperation.

papers.title: EasyOPD: An Easy-to-use On-Policy Distillation Framework for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Conventional language-model distillation often relies on fixed teacher-generated data, which may not cover the states encountered by an evolving student policy. On-policy distillation (OPD) instead collects teacher or evaluator supervision on student-generated rollouts. However, existing OPD methods differ substantially in supervision form, tokenizer compatibility, teacher access, and supervision granularity, leading to fragmented implementations that are difficult to reproduce and extend. We present \textsc{EasyOPD}, an on-policy distillation framework built on verl, a distributed reinforcement-learning framework for large language models. \textsc{EasyOPD} separates user-side configuration, method-specific supervision logic, and verl-based execution. Its method modules connect to the shared backend through extension boundaries for loss construction, rollout metadata, reward processing, tokenizer alignment, and teacher-side computation. We instantiate representative methods for three OPD settings -- cross-tokenizer OPD, on-policy self-distillation, and step-wise OPD. Experiments on reasoning, code-generation, scientific-knowledge, and tool-use benchmarks show that these implementations can be executed through the same verl-based backend while retaining their method-specific objectives and task-dependent performance profiles. We release \textsc{EasyOPD} with runnable YAML configurations, documentation, and an installable demonstration package and video.

papers.title: Inter-detector correlations in LIGO-Virgo strain: an exploratory study and possible astrophysical implications
papers.abstract: We investigate inter-detector correlations in public LIGO-Virgo strain around nine O2 and O3 events, using a band-pass-only statistic without waveform-template fitting. The primary sample comprises 27 event-pair measurements, with three complementary measurements for GW191127. Event-window maxima over $|\tau|\leq35$ ms are compared with 200 surrounding off-source maxima. With verified fractional catalog epochs, seven of the 27 primary event-pair measurements, all H1$\times$L1, reach the local finite-background floor $p=1/201$. No individual comparison passes a Holm correction at 5% for this family; the available background limits the attainable tail resolution. Complementary comparisons of simultaneous and time-displaced off-source data show processing-dependent structure, including a local excess near GW200219 that does not recur at comparable size in the additional segments examined. We discuss the possibility that part of the strain classified operationally as noise contains an astrophysical contribution, including an accumulated gravitational-radiation background associated with Bondi radiative processes.

papers.title: AgentAbstain: Do LLM Agents Know When Not to Act?
papers.abstract: Agent systems based on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for autonomous tasks, yet existing evaluations mostly focus on task success rather than whether agents know when to abstain. This gap poses real risks: under ambiguity, conflicting constraints, or tool failures, agents may execute unintended and irreversible actions. To close this gap, we present the first systematic evaluation framework for agentic abstention: the calibrated ability of tool-using LLM agents to recognize when not to act. At its core, AgentAbstain is a paired-task benchmark built on an agent-native taxonomy of 8 abstention scenarios across pre-execution reasoning and runtime discovery. It contains 263 paired tasks across 42 executable sandbox environments, where each pair consists of a should-act task and a should-abstain variant produced through a controlled perturbation to the instruction, tool, or environment state. To scale this paired design and resist data contamination, we propose AbstainGen, a fully automated pipeline that synthesizes sandbox environments and generates paired tasks end-to-end, validated by deterministic replay and semantic LLM judges; fresh task instances can be regenerated on demand, and three independent annotators rate 94-98% of sampled tasks as well-designed. Across 17 frontier LLMs in 4 agent harnesses, the best agent (Gemini 3.1 Pro) achieves only 59.5% paired accuracy (correct on both the act and abstain sides of each paired task). More importantly, abstention capability is largely independent of general task-solving capability, indicating that scaling task-solving alone will not close this gap. We further identify failure modes such as post-hoc abstention, in which agents execute irreversible actions before recognizing abstention triggers. Our code and dataset are open-sourced at agentabstain.github.io.

papers.title: Low-hard to high-soft spectral state transitions in the faintest early-X-ray-detected optical tidal disruption event TDE 2025aarm
papers.abstract: We report the X-ray and optical spectroscopic properties of TDE 2025aarm, the second closest tidal disruption event (TDE) discovered to date. The proximity of this source, combined with a deep and intense X-ray monitoring campaign spanning six months, allowed us to probe the source down to an unprecedented 0.2-10 keV luminosity of $\sim7\times10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$ close to the optical peak. This renders TDE 2025aarm the faintest early-X-ray-detected TDE to date. After the first X-ray detection, the source brightened by nearly two orders of magnitude, reaching a peak luminosity of $\sim5\times10^{41}$ erg s$^{-1}$ about four months after the optical peak. Through time-resolved X-ray spectral analysis, we find that TDE 2025aarm evolved from an initially hard, power-law-dominated X-ray state into a softer, disk-dominated state as the luminosity increased, before hardening again at later times. Such low-hard-to-high-soft state transitions are commonly observed in black hole X-ray binaries (XRBs) but have not previously been reported in thermal TDEs. We show that the spectral evolution can be described by variations in the relative contributions of an accretion disk and a Comptonizing component, qualitatively resembling the disk--corona evolution observed in XRBs. We also present the results of our optical spectroscopic follow-up campaign with HET/LRS2, confirming the TDE classification and revealing NIII Bowen fluorescence features. The extremely faint early-time X-ray emission of TDE 2025aarm further supports the idea that the historical dichotomy between X-ray-bright and X-ray-undetected TDEs is largely driven by selection effects related to the depth, cadence, and duration of X-ray follow-up observations. TDE 2025aarm therefore provides new insight into both the accretion physics of TDEs and the possible universality of accretion across several orders of magnitude in black hole mass.

papers.title: Predicting Lost Updates Is Not Enough to Choose a Rounding Policy
papers.abstract: In low-precision training, a weight can round back to its previous value after a small update. We test whether predicting how often this happens helps choose a rounding rule. In Pythia-410M continuations from a common checkpoint, a higher-precision pilot accurately predicted the fraction of matrix weights left unchanged at each of the first 64 updates. Across three schedules with optimizer state retained or reset, nearest rounding gave lower validation loss at 256 updates than stochastic rounding or retaining 32-bit weights. The same ordering held at 512 updates with retained state. Accurately forecasting the unchanged fraction did not identify a benefit from switching policies in these runs.

papers.title: Proof of Rump's Retraction Conjecture for Quasilinear Cycle Sets
papers.abstract: Nondegenerate cycle sets were introduced by Rump as an algebraic framework for nondegenerate, involutive solutions to the Yang--Baxter equation. Nondegenerate cycle set structures on abelian groups, such as translation-invariant and quasilinear cycle sets, are of particular interest when studying the retraction problem in the theory of the Yang--Baxter equation. In this article, we solve the retraction problem for finite quasilinear cycle sets by showing that each nontrivial quasilinear cycle set is retractable, thus proving a conjecture of Rump.

papers.title: Do Egocentric Video-Language Models Capture Both Hand- and Object-Centric Cues?
papers.abstract: Recognizing hand-object interactions (HOIs) requires capturing both hand dynamics and object transformations, which provide complementary information for distinguishing visually similar manipulations. However, Video-Language Models (VLMs) trained solely on egocentric videos tend to over-rely on hand appearance, struggling to distinguish interactions with similar visual appearances but different dynamics (e.g., taking vs. kneading dough). To better utilize complementary hand- and object-centric cues, we propose a learning paradigm with (i) hand-object masked training to encode both hand- and object-centric cues and learn their relationships through cross-cue reconstruction, and (ii) an HOI-dynamics-aware decoder that grounds each cue through auxiliary location and semantic predictions. To assess how effectively models leverage hand- and object-centric cues for action recognition, we introduce Cue-Isolated HOI (CI-HOI), which independently evaluates recognition performance based on each cue. To enable this evaluation, we curate the DEHOI testbed using video inpainting to selectively remove either hands or manipulated objects, allowing us to evaluate action recognition with each cue isolated. DEHOI reveals that existing VLMs trained only on egocentric video rely more on hand-centric cues than VLMs trained on more non-egocentric video data. We show that our training paradigm mitigates this hand-centric bias, outperforming VLMs trained on the same egocentric data across DEHOI, standard action recognition, and object state recognition benchmarks.

papers.title: Is Randomness Necessary for Adaptive Data Analysis?
papers.abstract: The Adaptive Data Analysis (ADA) problem formalizes the challenge of preventing false discovery and overfitting when a dataset is repeatedly reused. Formally, our input is a dataset containing $n$ i.i.d. samples from an unknown distribution $\mathcal{P}$ over a domain $\mathcal{X}$, and our goal is to answer a sequence of $k$ adaptively chosen statistical queries with respect to $\mathcal{P}$. The main question is how many queries we can support (i.e., how large $k$ can be), primarily as a function of the number of samples $n$. This question has been intensively studied and is relatively well-understood for randomized mechanisms: there are computationally efficient mechanisms that support $k \approx n^2$ queries, and no computationally efficient mechanism can answer $k \gg n^2$ queries. In this paper, we address a fundamental question: is randomness necessary for ADA? Despite a decade of work on ADA, this question remains open. A folklore observation dating back to the initial works on ADA is that randomness is {\em not} necessary when the analyst is computationally bounded. Yet, the necessity of randomness against computationally unbounded analysts has remained elusive. Our main contribution resolves this gap in the information-theoretic setting. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that randomness is {\em strictly necessary} to answer a non-trivial number of adaptive queries: when the analyst is unbounded, any deterministic mechanism can be forced to fail after just $k = \tilde{O}(n)$ queries.

papers.title: Memory-like effects and kinematics of trajectories in Cyclotron motion
papers.abstract: We investigate the collective dynamics of a bundle of charged particles undergoing cyclotron motion in a uniform magnetic field when subjected to a short-duration electric pulse. Using the geometric framework based on the evolution of trajectory congruences, we analyze how the pulse affects the expansion, shear, and rotation of a small family of trajectories. We show that the geometric imprint persists after the pulse has vanished, manifesting as a memory of the transient perturbation. Unlike gravitational memory effects, this does not manifest itself in focusing behaviour of the trajectories, and instead implies a restructuring of the shear component before and after the pulse. We offer direct analytic and regression based arguments for the same.

papers.title: Large language models create an uneven informational layer over cities
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are emerging as a new informational layer over cities, shaping which places people discover, consider, and ultimately visit. Yet little is known about which places they surface, which they ignore, and whether these patterns vary across communities and users and translate into real-world economic consequences. Here, we audit restaurant recommendations from five LLMs across 304 neighborhoods in five U.S. cities using 320 synthetic user profiles spanning income, age, sex, and residential status, issuing nearly one million queries. We find that LLMs both fabricate venues and systematically overlook real ones. Fabrication is concentrated in neighborhoods with weaker digital and physical footprints and virtually disappears when models are provided with verified venue lists. In contrast, invisibility persists: even when choosing from a fixed set of real venues, 41.5% of establishments are never recommended, and nearly one-fifth of venues are overlooked by all five models, indicating that uneven visibility reflects not only missing knowledge but also systematic patterns of selective attention that are shared across models. The same selectivity extends to users. Within identical venue pools, higher-income users receive more expensive and less popular venues, while tourists are directed toward costlier but more socially diverse establishments than local residents. Simulating the resulting shifts in consumer demand suggests that widespread reliance on LLM recommendations would redirect visits and revenue away from chain and quick-service restaurants toward independent and full-service dining. Together, our findings show that LLMs act as a selective layer of urban information that unevenly distributes visibility across places and people, with potential consequences for local economies and urban inequality.

papers.title: RABBiT: Rapidly adaptive BOLD foundation model via brain-tuning for accurate zero-shot and few-shot prediction of speech-elicited responses in the brain
papers.abstract: Language understanding in the brain is context-dependent, varying across experimental stimuli and individuals, which makes it difficult to build computational models that generalize across both. This calls for a foundation model of language-evoked brain activity that can capture shared structure while adapting efficiently to new participants and inputs. We introduce RABBiT (Rapidly Adaptive BOLD foundation model via BraIn-Tuning), a compact audio-to-fMRI encoder designed for accurate zero- and few-shot prediction. A comprehensive evaluation on 324 participants across multiple unseen fMRI datasets shows that RABBiT enables accurate zero-shot prediction of fMRI responses to natural speech across auditory and language-selective regions, surpassing the SOTA foundation model for fMRI and predictions based on group averages. With as little as 10 minutes of participant-specific data, RABBiT further improves performance via parameter-efficient tuning, substantially outperforming per-participant linear models. RABBiT's performance is driven by two key innovations: (1) learned region-specific attention, and (2) a decomposition of brain responses into shared and subject-specific components, combined with a brain-tuned speech backbone. In addition to supporting strong predictive accuracy, the structured, region-specific representations that RABBiT learns enable interpretability. By eliminating the need for extensive per-participant data and model fitting, RABBiT enables scalable population-level analyses of language in the human brain. We make the code available at https://github.com/bridge-ai-neuro/rabbit.

papers.title: Uncertainty-aware damage identification in short-span bridges via physics-informed variational autoencoder
papers.abstract: Vibration-based damage identification in civil infrastructure is a challenging, ill-posed inverse problem due to measurement noise, sparse sensor arrays, and modeling errors. While deep learning is powerful for system identification, deterministic approaches lack reliable uncertainty quantification and can yield physically inconsistent results. This work proposes a probabilistic Scientific Machine Learning framework for structural health monitoring: a physics-informed Gaussian copula variational autoencoder. The methodology introduces two main contributions. First, a numerical eigenvalue solver is embedded directly into the variational autoencoder as its decoder, which replaces data-driven surrogates, ensures that every posterior sample satisfies the governing equations of structural dynamics, and reduces the number of trainable parameters. Second, a Gaussian copula describes the posterior distribution of the stiffness factors, capturing cross-correlations between components with fewer parameters than Gaussian mixtures in real time. We validate the method numerically on a short-span bridge supported on elastic bearings, whose response is dominated by vertical bending, accounting for modeling errors, measurement noise, and a finer finite element discretization for testing. The method estimates the posterior distribution of the damage condition, i.e., the stiffness reduction factors of the deck zones and bearings, and these posteriors closely match the exact ones computed with sequential Monte Carlo sampling. The results reveal that the proposed methodology offers a robust and interpretable decision-making tool, able not only to indicate the presence and location of damage, but also to inform on the uncertainty associated with the diagnosis, for instance, when light damage is masked by the effect of noise or when the measured modal properties present limited sensitivity to damage.

papers.title: When Do Foundation Models Pay Off? A Break-Even Analysis of Pretrained Time Series Forecasters
papers.abstract: Deploying a time series foundation model (FM) requires GPU infrastructure and engineering overhead, with no guarantee of improvement over classical forecasting methods. We provide the first systematic break-even analysis of when this investment pays off. Across 30 benchmark datasets, we compare zero-shot and LoRA fine-tuned FMs (Chronos-Bolt, Moirai, Lag-Llama) against classical baselines (Naive, ETS, ARIMA, XGBoost) at six training set sizes from 2% to 100% of available data. FMs outperform classical methods at every evaluated training fraction on 16 of 30 datasets. On 6 datasets, classical methods surpass zero-shot FMs with at most 5% of the training data (21--6,324 samples); on the remaining 8, break-even ranges from 24 to 22,177 samples. No classical method dominates: ARIMA, Naive, ETS and XGBoost are each best on 6--11 datasets. One robust rule requires no model training: if n_train < 700 and seasonality is non-negligible, FM zero-shot is the right low-data choice -- below 20% of the history, classical methods either lose to it (4 of these 10 datasets) or cannot be fitted at all (6) -- and it stays best at full history on 6 of them; fine-tuning should be skipped. Contrary to common practice, LoRA fine-tuning rarely helps and degrades short series by up to 52%. We operationalise these findings as a two-step decision framework -- compute dataset length and seasonality strength, run a brief 5--10% pilot only if needed. Cheap dataset features do not predict the break-even category at this benchmark scale, so outside the rule a pilot remains necessary. Code and benchmark: https://github.com/nicolaisi/fm_breakeven.

papers.title: Fooling Yourself: how narratives shape beliefs
papers.abstract: Narratives often combine diagnostic evidence with truthful but nondiagnostic details. In a two-state experiment with known signal likelihoods, we test whether such details distort belief updating. Although Bayes' rule prescribes no revision, nondiagnostic signals induce revisions consistent with considering both states equally likely. Such revisions are most frequent when nondiagnostic signals appear as clues in a story, less frequent in an abstract urn problem, and virtually absent when the same story replaces these clues with explicit no-information messages. Simulations show that these revisions reduce belief accuracy and delay decisions, an effect communicators could exploit without lying.

papers.title: Aura: Consistent Multi-Subject Video Generation via VLM-Grounded Semantic Alignment
papers.abstract: Subject-driven and multi-element video generation are central to controllable video synthesis, but existing methods still struggle to preserve identity consistency and model complex relationships among multiple subjects. In this paper, we propose Aura, a unified framework for high-fidelity and identity-consistent video generation. To better capture scene dynamics and subject interactions, we introduce AI director-level captions that provide dense and structured descriptions of video content. We further leverage a vision-language model (VLM) with learnable queries to extract multimodal semantic features from textual and visual references, covering both global semantics and fine-grained visual cues. To bridge the representational gap between the VLM and the Diffusion Transformer (DiT), we design a two-stage alignment strategy that progressively maps VLM features into the DiT feature space. For visual conditioning, we adopt token concatenation to inject reference information directly into the generation process. To distinguish heterogeneous subject types and reduce common copy-paste artifacts, we develop a subject-aware RoPE-Shift mechanism. To further differentiate reference images of different categories, we introduce subject-aware learnable tokens. In addition, we introduce Memory Tokens to balance the training signal across examples with different numbers of reference subjects. During inference, Progressive-APG (Adaptive Prompt Guidance) further alleviates oversaturation and improves semantic alignment with user prompts. Finally, we build a high-quality video-subject image dataset through a dedicated data construction pipeline. Extensive experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both single-subject generation and more challenging multi-element scenarios.

papers.title: Neural LiDAR Bundle Adjustment
papers.abstract: Recent research has achieved remarkable novel view rendering and scene reconstruction results with Neural Radiance Field (NeRF), including extensions to the LiDAR modality. Few studies have, however, explored the key design differences between RGB NeRFs and LiDAR NeRFs, particularly considering their underlying working principles. In this work, we provide both theoretical and empirical evidence suggesting that the density of volume sampling plays a significant role in LiDAR NeRF. Based on this finding, we propose a novel Neural LiDAR Bundle Adjustment (NeLD-BA) algorithm, which is tailored using efficient volume sampling of LiDAR rays for joint optimization of LiDAR map and poses. Extensive experiments are performed using the Newer College and FusionPortable datasets to demonstrate the proposed NeLD-BA's state-of-the-art performance in multi-view point cloud registration and 3D mapping. We will open-source our code for the community.

papers.title: SPIRAL-360: Stratified Panoramic Instruction Replay and Angular Learning for Visual Grounding
papers.abstract: Localizing targets in $360^\circ$ environments requires combining global context with fine-grained evidence despite projection distortion and horizontal wrap-around. Uneven directional coverage compounds these challenges, particularly for seam-adjacent and polar targets. We present SPIRAL-360, a geometry-aware framework with separately trained single-turn and multi-turn models for panoramic localization. Spherically Stratified Replay (SSR) broadens directional coverage through stratified sampling and consistent transformations of panoramas, target annotations, and tool trajectories. TapSphere incorporates spherical distance priors into panoramic visual attention, while Spherical Direction Regularization (SDR) complements coordinate-token prediction with auxiliary direction supervision during training. The single-turn model predicts directly from the panorama, while the multi-turn model inspects tool-generated perspective views. We construct SPIRAL-360 Search, a curated dataset of trajectories interleaving reasoning, projection actions, and visual observations. Both models undergo full-parameter supervised fine-tuning followed by policy optimization. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art localization on S360 and competitive cross-dataset transfer, including H$^*$Bench. Systematic ablations support the effectiveness of this geometric learning design.

papers.title: Foliations by constant spacetime mean curvature surfaces for asymptotically hyperboloidal initial data sets
papers.abstract: We construct an exhaustive family of constant spacetime mean curvature (STCMC) surfaces for initial data sets close to the anti-de Sitter-Schwarzschild hyperboloid. In particular, we obtain such a foliation as the long time limit of the volume preserving spacetime mean curvature flow starting from the constant mean curvature foliation constructed by Neves-Tian (Geom. Funct. Anal., 2009). As an application, inspired by the definition of STCMC center of mass for initial data sets proposed in the asymptotically Euclidean setting by Cederbaum-Sakovich (Calc. Var. PDE, 2021), we study the center of mass of an asymptotically hyperboloidal initial data set.

papers.title: Insecurity of Measurement-Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution
papers.abstract: The security of practical quantum key distribution (QKD) systems is fundamentally constrained by vulnerabilities of single-photon detectors. Measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) was proposed to remove this limitation by allowing all measurements to be performed by a completely untrusted party, under the assumption that the measurement node can be treated as adversarial but does not compromise the security guarantees of the protocol. Here we show that this assumption is insufficient under realistic adversarial control of the measurement device. We present an attack in which an adversary exploits active control of the measurement node (Charlie) to obtain significant information about the secret key. The attack enables recovery of up to 70\% of the sifted key while introducing only 5.6\% quantum bit error rate. Unlike previously reported attacks targeting specific implementations of MDI-QKD, our results demonstrate a limitation of the standard security model underlying the protocol. These findings indicate that additional constraints on the measurement-device independence assumption, or refined security analyses incorporating stronger adversarial capabilities, are required to ensure the security of MDI-QKD in realistic scenarios.

papers.title: ElephantAgent: Contextual State Continuity in Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: Agentic systems enhance their capabilities by invoking external tools and maintaining persistent memory. However, recent tool and memory poisoning attacks can covertly bias agent behavior. We observe that such attacks mounted out of band share a single enabler: each succeeds only by presenting the agent with a contextual state (e.g., tool state and memory) that is not the latest faithfully evolved one. This observation suggests that a continuity check over the contextual state covers this family of attacks. We present ElephantAgent, a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity over the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's context. Before each planning-and-execution cycle, ElephantAgent recomputes the digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest in a linearizable ledger of state transitions, maintained over replicated trusted hardware. The protocol also provides Historical Traceability, a secondary guarantee that keeps state transitions attributable and recoverable. We integrate ElephantAgent into DeepSeek Harness (DSH) and implement ElephantDSH, an agentic system protected by contextual state verification. ElephantDSH withstood all out-of-band attack attempts, from rug pulls and rollbacks to attacks on its own mechanism, and recovered from an in-band prompt injection in all trials. By comparison, existing defenses typically check only what enters the context: of the five we evaluated, all leaked the targeted content under the rollback, and three also under the rug pull. ElephantDSH completed all normal coding tasks with a relative overhead of 1.02-1.07$\times$ over the original DSH with model latency variation removed.

papers.title: The Intrinsic Inertia, Droop, and Nonlinear Stability of Observer-Synchronized Grid-Forming Control
papers.abstract: Observer-synchronized (OBS) grid-forming (GFM) control, in which grid synchronization, active-power regulation, voltage-magnitude regulation, and current limiting are integrated into a unified observer-based structure, was proposed in recent years as an alternative to conventional GFM control such as droop control. Existing research on OBS GFM mainly focuses on its linearized modelling, small-signal stability, and parameter sensitivity, while a nonlinear analysis, which characterizes its inertia, droop characteristics, and nonlinear convergence, is currently absent. This paper develops a systematic nonlinear analysis of OBS control. First, a second-order nonlinear autonomous model is derived under the quasi-steady-state assumption. The intrinsic inertia is characterized through an exact nonlinear swing-equation representation, while the nonlinear droop characteristics are derived from the steady-state relations. These results provide guidelines for controller parameterization. Furthermore, the equilibrium points and nonlinear stability properties are investigated using the qualitative theory of differential equations, giving explicit criteria to guarantee almost global asymptotic stability of the desired equilibriums. The analysis is validated through detailed electromagnetic transient simulations and hardware experiments.

papers.title: FPGA-based LQG controller and hardware-in-the-loop simulator implementation for nanomechanical systems
papers.abstract: We present an open-source framework for real-time Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulation on the affordable Red Pitaya STEMlab FPGA platform. The controller implements a discrete-time Kalman filter and Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) for systems with up to three coupled oscillatory degrees of freedom, targeting applications in levitated optomechanics, MEMS/NEMS, and related experimental platforms. Complementing the controller, the HIL simulator provides a~configurable second-order stochastic plant with nonlinear input and output mappings, enabling realistic closed-loop testing under real-time and fixed-point constraints. A MATLAB-based workflow automates model configuration, controller synthesis, numerical scaling, and FPGA deployment without requiring specialized hardware expertise. As an end-to-end demonstration, we present the stabilization of a levitated nanoparticle in a two-dimensional double-well potential, illustrating the complete workflow from model definition and simulation to real-time feedback control. The codebase: https://github.com/TU-Wien-ACIN-CDS/FPGA-based-LQG-and-HIL-simulator-for-nanomechanical-systems

papers.title: When Does Learning to Stop Help? Configuring Risk-Controlled Early Exit for Reasoning-Model Services
papers.abstract: Early exit lowers the cost of serving a reasoning model by stopping its reasoning once a provisional answer looks final. An operator must choose between a learned stopping rule and one static token budget, and savings against full reasoning do not settle the choice. We present a procedure that decides on calibration data from the workload. It certifies both families with Learn-then-Test to one bound on the fraction of all questions that full reasoning answers correctly but early exit does not, prices provisional answers as the serving stack does, and deploys the cheapest certified candidate. Across four models and five benchmarks neither family is better throughout. At a 5% risk target the learned rule saves 10.4-17.0 percentage points more tokens than the static budget on free-form mathematics with Qwen3, with accuracy 2.4-2.9 points below full reasoning, and less on MMLU-Pro on average. Which family costs less also changes with the risk target, in 8 of 15 settings, and with the price of a provisional answer. Across three prices, committing to one family in advance gives up as much as 27.4 points on some workload, whereas selecting on calibration data falls at most 11.6 points short of the better family, on a task with only 99 calibration questions. In a vLLM engine with Qwen3-8B, mean response time fell in proportion to generated tokens. Policies served on a task other than their calibration task exceeded the risk target in 18 of 44 task pairs; recalibration on the new task restored risk control.
authors: Zhe Dong (University of Maine at Presque Isle)

papers.title: Compaction function in stochastic inflation: a FOREST of type I and II primordial black holes
papers.abstract: We show how to compute the compaction function within stochastic inflation, by solving the random field dynamics on stochastic binary trees. In this framework, the compaction function is directly related to the ratio of the volumes emerging from the sibling and child branches of a given node. This construction also determines whether or not the areal radius of a perturbation increases monotonically with the radial coordinate, thereby distinguishing between type-I and type-II fluctuations. As an application, we investigate primordial black hole (PBH) formation in a single-field toy model with a constant potential slope, using stochastic-tree realizations generated with the public code FOREST. In the classical regime, where quantum diffusion is subdominant, the PBH mass function is narrowly distributed and type-II fluctuations are strongly suppressed relative to type I. By contrast, in the quantum and near-critical (i.e. close to eternal inflation) regimes, the PBH mass distribution spans several orders of magnitude, the overall PBH abundance is enhanced, and type-II fluctuations outnumber type I. In that case cloud-in-cloud effects are also important, highlighting the need for a better understanding of the evolution and collapse of type-II fluctuations in order to obtain robust PBH predictions when stochastic effects are significant.

papers.title: Know Before You Fetch: When Does Confidence-Based Retrieval-Budget Allocation Pay Off?
papers.abstract: Adaptive retrieval-augmented generation uses a signal from the reader, such as its confidence when answering without retrieval (closed-book), to decide whether and how much to retrieve. We compare such methods not with always retrieving many passages but with the best simple policy under the same cap on average passages per query: a fixed depth or a random mixture of fixed depths. Policies allocate zero, one or five passages and are scored on held-out questions. Seven settings of about 2,000 questions combine TriviaQA, Natural Questions and MS MARCO, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B readers, and two retrieval sources: per-question passage pools and a 3.5-million-passage Wikipedia index. Allocation by confidence could gain in three ways. It rations a scarce budget: at a cap of half a passage per query it beats the best simple policy in all seven settings, by 0.010 to 0.075 in accuracy. It avoids harmful retrieval: at caps of one passage or more, substantial gains appear only on Wikipedia, where passages often overwrite known answers, most robustly for Qwen3-8B on TriviaQA (+0.051, also under exact match and F1). It barely helps to choose depth: closed-book confidence ranks which queries a first passage helps but ranks the choice between one and five passages little better than chance, and with passage pools a fixed depth of two or three passages is as good or better. Once the probe's latency is charged, gains remain only where the gate skips retrieval for most queries; for the larger reader they also depend on the answer metric.

papers.title: Finite-resolution exhaustive traversal of thermodynamic state spaces has divergent thermodynamic length
papers.abstract: Resolving a prescribed multidimensional control window by a single continuous, serial scan is a task distinct from driving between fixed endpoints. We formulate this task as metric coverage at resolution $\eps$. Classical covering estimates, applied to a compact regular $d$-dimensional Riemannian window, give a required length of order at least $\eps^{1-d}$; local grid traversals attain the same exponent. When a physical friction tensor uniformly dominates the coverage metric, this geometric cost implies a necessary duration of order at least $\eps^{-2(d-1)}$ at fixed quadratic excess-work budget. Fixed-duration divergence refers to the slow-driving quadratic action and is not a claim about exact work outside that regime. A detailed-balance three-state process and an overdamped harmonic trap provide microscopic friction examples. For the trap, independently integrated Gaussian moment dynamics approach the quadratic prediction as the prescribed raster is slowed, while refinement at a controlled work budget increases scan duration. A quasi-uniform operational resolution floor cuts off the geometric divergence. Landau-response and van der Waals proxy metrics serve separately as prescribed diagnostic geometries: independent quadrature tests their coordinate- and protocol-dependent critical prefactors without asserting universal critical dissipation. Morton ordering supplies an ordering/connector benchmark with larger finite-resolution amplitudes. The resulting resource statements apply to exhaustive serial coverage, with metric, interpolation and driving assumptions specified explicitly.

papers.title: How additional labels affect multiparticle indistinguishability of identical particles
papers.abstract: For two identical particles, adding labels reduces the total overlap of their label states and decreases their exchange indistinguishability as measured by Hong--Ou--Mandel interference. For more than two particles, the opposite effect can occur: introducing additional labels can boost multiparticle indistinguishability. We present an explicit seven-particle example in which additional labels increase multiparticle indistinguishability by $7.38\%$, as quantified by the symmetric projection weight of the seven-particle label state, while decreasing the mean squared pairwise overlap by nearly half. We trace this effect to the cancellation of collective multiparticle phases. Phases associated with one set of label states cancel those associated with the other, thereby turning destructive contributions to the symmetric weight into constructive ones. We also give sufficient conditions that rule out this effect. For any number of identical particles, additional label states independent of the original label states cannot increase indistinguishability when the original symmetric weight is at least $1/2$. Independent additional label states also cannot increase the symmetric weight of any number of identical particles prepared independently in the same mixed label state.

papers.title: Brownian Bridge Diffusion-Assisted Joint Channel Estimation and Data Detection for Jamming-Resilient OFDM Receivers
papers.abstract: In next-generation wireless networks, the growing density of devices and limited spectrum resources pose severe jamming challenges to fragile legitimate communication links in the wireless electromagnetic environment. Crucially, when jamming overlaps with pilot and data symbols in both time and frequency domains, it inflicts a severe bottleneck on receiver-side joint estimation and detection. Existing schemes often lack an effective framework to combat such jamming contamination, thereby failing to guarantee reliable transmission. To address this issue, we propose a Brownian bridge diffusion-assisted joint channel estimation and data detection (BBD-JCED) framework for jamming-resilient orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) receivers. The proposed framework consists of a jamming suppression module and a Brownian bridge-joint recovery module. The former identifies jamming-contaminated bins in the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) domain and suppresses the dominant jamming components through spectral notching. The latter establishes a Brownian bridge-based probabilistic graph to model the probabilistic transition process from the suppressed OFDM observation to the coded bits, and performs a reverse recovery process to enable enhanced joint channel estimation and data detection. Moreover, we derive a variational lower bound (VLB) to reformulate the intractable bit estimate problem into a tractable training objective, providing a probabilistic foundation for the loss function design. Furthermore, we develop a two-stage training algorithm to separately optimize the jamming suppression and Brownian bridge-joint recovery modules. Simulation results under representative jamming types demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior jamming suppression and bit recovery performance over the considered baseline schemes while maintaining competitive inference complexity.

papers.title: FlexMoE: Learning One-for-All Multi-Budget Expert Pruning for Flexible MoE Deployment
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models scale model capacity through sparse expert activation, yet deployment still requires storing and serving all experts. Moreover, deployment budgets can vary substantially across devices, users, and workloads. Existing MoE compression methods typically optimize a separate compressed model for each target budget. We introduce FlexMoE, a post-training one-for-all framework that converts a large pretrained MoE model into a multi-budget family of smaller deployable subnetworks. FlexMoE first ranks expert FFN channels by importance to construct a sliceable weight space shared across budgets, and then learns expert-wise discrete retention actions under gradually increasing cost pressure, allowing a single action-training run to produce reliable pruning masks across budgets. Moreover, only a single mid-budget fine-tune can further recover degraded performance and yields a shared recovered model that transfers to other unseen budgets, avoiding repeated per-budget recovery and separated checkpoint storage. Across tested MoE LLMs with diverse architectures and scales, FlexMoE consistently outperforms strong MoE compression baselines. In particular, on Qwen2-57B-A14B, it retains ~99.8% of base performance while pruning 50% of routed-expert parameters even without recovery fine-tuning. For deployment, pruned subnetworks deliver real memory reduction and end-to-end throughput gains, while our kernel co-design enables runtime budget switching without checkpoint reloading and delivers substantial inference acceleration.

papers.title: MSA-3D: Rotation Curves and Dark Matter Fractions at z~0.5-1.7 with JWST/NIRSpec
papers.abstract: We present rotation curves and inner mass distributions for 30 star-forming galaxies at $0.5<z<1.7$, down to stellar masses of $\sim10^9\,M_\odot$, observed with JWST/NIRSpec in the MSA-3D Cycle 1 survey. We combine spatially resolved ionised-gas kinematics and JWST/NIRCam imaging in forward dynamical models to constrain baryonic and dark matter contributions. The 24 golden-sample galaxies exhibit ordered rotation, with intrinsic dispersions of $\sigma_0\simeq34$--63~km\,s$^{-1}$ and median $V_{\rm rot}/\sigma_0=2.9$ at $2.2R_{\rm s}$. Their stellar Tully--Fisher relation has a slope consistent with previous $z\sim1$ studies ($a=3.8\pm0.5$) but substantial inter-survey differences in normalisation. Within the disk effective radius, we obtain a median dark matter fraction $f_{\rm DM}(R_e)=0.73$ (68\% range: 0.49--0.84), with systematic dependence on the adopted baryonic mass scale. Across comparison surveys, $f_{\rm DM}(R_e)$ correlates more strongly with baryonic surface density than stellar mass, although neither trend is significant within MSA-3D. Five galaxies favour inner halo slopes shallower than NFW (versus $\approx2$ expected by chance), three significantly in model-matched NFW injection tests. Among 16 galaxies with sufficient radial coverage, five have rising, eight flat, and three falling rotation curves (although individual slopes are mostly not significant), with no clear dependence on other properties. Together, these results indicate that these low-mass disks at $z\sim1$ are dark-matter dominated within $R_e$ for the baryonic mass scale favoured by the kinematics, although adopting the catalogue-based masses lowers the median to $\approx0.5$. Their inner halo profiles are generally consistent with or moderately shallower than NFW. These observations demonstrate the efficiency of JWST for extending resolved dynamical studies to lower-mass galaxies.

papers.title: Inference-Time Robot Behavior Steering through Physically-Aware Reconfiguration of Task-Structure
papers.abstract: A central challenge in deploying robot policies is inference-time policy steering: redirecting a policy to satisfy natural-language preferences unseen in training, without retraining. Existing methods fail in two modes: end-to-end policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) require fine-tuning or expert-level guidance, while neuro-symbolic methods rely on predefined symbols whose edits can yield logically valid but physically infeasible plans. We propose ReStruct, a zero-shot method built on a neural automaton policy that decomposes a visuomotor policy into a high-level state-machine skeleton and a low-level residual controller. A vision-language model (VLM) grounds the preference in the skeleton's learned symbols, refining them if needed, and compiles it into a temporal-logic automaton, whose synchronous product with the skeleton reconfigures the task structure. With the controller frozen, the skeleton's action priors are updated for physically-aware control. In simulation and real-world experiments, ReStruct steers preferences from object-centric specifications to temporal-logic constraints, including novel combinations of demonstrated behaviors that require compositional generalization. Average preference-following success is 70.9% in simulation and 92.5% on a real robot, surpassing baselines like the prompt-steered vision-language-action model {\pi}0.5.

papers.title: SharQ: Bridging Activation Sparsity and FP4 Quantization for LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Low-bit floating-point formats and semi-structured sparsity are increasingly supported by modern accelerators, yet combining them for LLM activation compression remains challenging: activations contain input-dependent outliers that dominate block scales in FP4 quantization, and directly applying N:M sparsity masks discards moderate values, coupling sparsification loss with quantization error. We introduce SharQ, a training-free inference method that bridges activation sparsity and FP4 quantization through an online sparse--dense decomposition. For each activation tensor, SharQ generates an input-adaptive N:M mask to extract an outlier-dominated sparse backbone, quantizes it to FP4, and defines a dense residual relative to the quantized sparse backbone rather than the unquantized sparse values. A sparse FP4 GEMM processes the backbone while a dense FP4 GEMM compensates for both mask-induced activation loss and sparse-path quantization error. The two paths share a single FP4 weight payload with path-specific scale views, and a fused preparation kernel absorbs mask generation, residual construction, and layer normalization into one operator. SharQ requires no calibration data, retraining, or model-specific tuning. Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Qwen3-VL-8B, SharQ recovers 43--63% of the NVFP4-to-FP16 accuracy gap across language and vision-language tasks, and generalizes across NVFP4, HiF4, and MXFP4 formats. On an RTX 5090, SharQ delivers 2.2--2.4$\times$ latency reduction over FP16 and 1.2--1.4$\times$ throughput improvement over FP8 in language model serving, and up to 1.58$\times$ speedup on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B video generation when combined with SageAttention. Our code is available at https://github.com/actypedef/SharQ.

papers.title: Multi-Modal Environment-Aware Beam Management for Massive MIMO: A Geometry-Driven Virtual Base Station Framework
papers.abstract: High-frequency massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems promise ultra-high data rates. However, efficient beam management remains challenging due to the prohibitive beam training overhead and intricate coordination required in multi-user MIMO (MU-MIMO) scenarios. To address these bottlenecks, environment-aware communications have emerged as a promising paradigm, leveraging site-specific knowledge to circumvent exhaustive pilot-based beam training and streamline multi-user communications. In this paper, we propose a geometry-driven framework that utilizes multi-modal environmental data, specifically regional 3D light detection and ranging (LiDAR) point clouds and location information, to construct an offline virtual base station (VBS) database. By modeling dominant reflection paths via mirror symmetry across building facades reconstructed from the point clouds, the VBS database provides a compact and sparse description of the wireless propagation environment. Given a user location, the VBS representation supports online coarse channel reconstruction and the generation of a beamspace prior. To refine the coarse estimates, we design a VBS-assisted orthogonal-pilot (VOP)-based partial beam training scheme with limited online measurements. Finally, to coordinate beam selection under inter-user interference, we develop a hierarchical dual-agent dueling double deep Q-network for coordinated beam selection (DD3QN-CBS). Simulation results show that the proposed framework improves effective spectral efficiency over the evaluated stochastic, heuristic, and conventional learning-based baselines, while achieving competitive performance with fewer online beam measurements.

papers.title: Embedding Foundation Model Predictions in Discrete-Choice Models with Structural Guarantees
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models achieve strong accuracy on choice prediction tasks, but their predictions often violate the economic logic those tasks require: raising a price can increase predicted demand, implied estimates of willingness to pay are frequently negative or implausible, and unavailable alternatives receive nonzero probability. We propose TabFM-Logit, an adapter that takes a foundation model's predicted choice probabilities as a precomputed feature and embeds them inside a multinomial logit's utility. In Stage 1, we fit the multinomial logit's structural coefficients by maximum likelihood with sign constraints. In Stage 2, we freeze those coefficients and fit a small neural correction operating on the foundation model's predictions. We prove that this composition exactly preserves the multinomial logit's marginal rate of substitution, so the analytically computable value of time becomes a mathematical guarantee rather than an empirical accident, and that training the two stages jointly breaks identifiability of the structural coefficients. Counterfactual derivatives and response signs are therefore the multinomial logit's by construction, and the foundation model contributes accuracy on observed choices. On respondents and households unseen in training, the adapter gains 5.7-6.8 percentage points (pp) of test accuracy on Swissmetro, 1.5 pp on LPMC, and 3.3-3.6 pp on IoT-Wearables over the multinomial logit (4.2 pp on average), stays within 1.0 pp of the raw foundation model, maintains 100% cost monotonicity, and keeps the multinomial logit's values of time exactly. The gain is largest where the multinomial logit is weakest and smallest where it is already strong. In every case it comes with the multinomial logit's guarantees, which the raw foundation models lack.

papers.title: Bobkingite, a new coupled sawtooth chain platform
papers.abstract: We investigate the mineral bobkingite, $\mathrm{Cu}_5(\mathrm{OH})_8\mathrm{Cl}_2(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_2$, as a potential realization of the sawtooth chain. Using ab initio methods, we estimate the magnetic exchange couplings and find that bobkingite hosts quasi-one-dimensional sawtooth chains, with residual three-dimensional interactions strongly suppressed by the crystal geometry. Examining the full exchange network, we find that the classical model exhibits an extensive manifold of nearly degenerate states with emergent two-dimensional character, which spin-wave theory shows to persist as Ising degrees of freedom. Unlike other sawtooth candidates, bobkingite has negligible vertical interchain coupling, preserving a one-dimensional degeneracy even in the presence of ordering, suggesting that any long-range order is weak. Thermal fluctuations stabilize a finite-temperature regime of multiplanar fluctuations rooted in the classical chain degeneracy, whose spin correlations resemble those of the quantum sawtooth chain, suggesting the persistence of quantum features in the full model. This makes bobkingite a compelling platform for exploring sawtooth chain physics.

papers.title: V-Zero: Gating On-Policy Distillation with Contrastive Visual Evidence for Fine-Grained Visual Reasoning
papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual reasoning requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to identify task-relevant visual evidence and ground their reasoning in local image regions. Existing methods typically rely on reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards or supervised fine-tuning on large-scale annotated reasoning traces, resulting in costly exploration, hand-designed verification rules, or heavy dependence on textual supervision. While On-Policy Distillation (OPD) offers a promising alternative via dense teacher supervision, its token-level objective inherently focuses on local token corrections, failing to assess global trajectory quality. In this work, we first reinterpret OPD as a stop-gradient alignment objective, revealing that its potential is limited by the absence of trajectory-level discrimination. Motivated by this observation, we propose V-Zero, which gates on-policy distillation with contrastive visual evidence. Specifically, V-Zero evaluates each trajectory under paired positive and negative visual views; the resulting likelihood contrast forms a trajectory-level gate that selectively amplifies updates from visually well-supported reasoning paths while suppressing ungrounded ones. Experiments on multiple visual reasoning and perception benchmarks show that V-Zero improves the Qwen3.5-4B backbone by 3.9 points on average while preserving strong generalization. Notably, V-Zero achieves more than 3$\times$ and 6$\times$ training speedups over representative supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning baselines, respectively. It requires neither annotated textual reasoning traces nor external reward signals. Code and dataset are released at https://github.com/eVI-group-SCU/V-Zero.

papers.title: Programmable Probabilistic Computer with 1,000,000 p-bits
papers.abstract: Many problems in physics and machine learning require sampling the collective states of large numbers of interacting variables. On modern graphics processors, repeated movement of interaction data between memory and compute units can limit how efficiently these calculations can scale. Here we demonstrate a programmable probabilistic computer with one million interacting probabilistic bits (p-bits) across 18 field-programmable gate arrays, sustaining $10^{12}$ probabilistic updates per second. Coupling weights remain beside the update circuits in on-chip memory, and only single-bit boundary states pass between devices. Experiments on three-dimensional and quasi-two-dimensional spin glasses show that the ratio of boundary-exchange frequency to local update frequency controls the effect of communication delays on optimization. A bound derived from the graph partition and interconnect identifies operating conditions that recover the residual-energy decay of an unpartitioned GPU reference. Infrequent exchange reduces the decay exponent, although faster local updates can shorten the time to reach a target energy. A cluster mean-field model reproduces this dependence, while ferromagnetic sampling experiments reveal a corresponding dependence of magnetization relaxation on the same frequency ratio. These results establish a million-p-bit computing architecture in which processing and local memory scale together, and provide a quantitative design principle for exploiting tolerance to communication delays in larger probabilistic computers.

papers.title: Autonomous Video Generation for Self-Evolving World Models
papers.abstract: Large-scale video generation models are increasingly described as world models because they can learn rich spatiotemporal regularities from visual data. We argue that an ideal world model should benefit in a self-evolving generative character. As such, a self-evolving world model can be realized via a generative model conditioned by various constraints, whose future predictions are refined through feedback. However, traditional visually plausible predictions alone are not enough to establish whether an imagined future is physically actionable for a particular embodied agent, failing to provide informative feedback from environments for self-evolving improvement. To realize self-evolving world models, this article proposes the concept of autonomous video generation, which is evaluated through counterfactual controllability, i.e., the ability to i) generate intervention-conditioned futures, ii) bind these future frames to embodiment constraints, iii) verify them under distribution shifts, and iv) distil surviving branches into compact variables for decision-making. We formalize a four-stage closed-loop optimization of Generation, Binding, Verification and Distillation, together with four corresponding evaluation metrics: novelty, consistency, out-of-distribution (OOD) and efficiency. We further discuss two examples, i.e., drones and manipulators, as early embodied testbeds where wind, sensing limits, actuation delay, contact dynamics and recovery constraints can be systematically perturbed and verified. The central claim is that the framework of autonomous video generation for self-evolving world models should not be judged by video fidelity alone, but by whether the generated frames improve valid action under counterfactual interventions and various embodiment constraints.

papers.title: General Lagrangian formulations for mixed-antisymmetric tensor fields on flat backgrounds
papers.abstract: We present, for the first time, local Lagrangian formulations for (ir)reducible integer higher-spin massless and massive Poincare group representations subject to Young tableau with $k$ columns $Y[\hat{s}_1,\hat{s}_2,...,\hat{s}_k]$ in $d$-dimensional Minkowski space-time. The particles are described in a metric-like formulation by tensor fields carrying $k$ groups of antisymmetric Lorentz indices $\Phi_{\mu^1[{\hat{s}_1}],\mu^2[{\hat{s}_2}],..., \mu^k[{\hat{s}_k}]}$ using the BRST procedure with both the complete operator $Q$ and incomplete $Q_c$ BRST operators. Starting from a description of bosonic mixed-antisymmetric higher-spin fields in terms of an auxiliary Fock space associated with a special Poincare module, we realize a conversion of the initial operator constraint system into a system of first-class operator constraints. For this purpose, we find, for the first time, by means of Verma module the auxiliary representations of the constraint subalgebra, to be isomorphic due to Howe duality to $so(k,k)$ algebra, and containing the subsystem of second-class operators in terms of new oscillator variables forming the Fock module. An unconstrained (with $Q$) and constrained (with $Q_c$ and BRST invariant algebraic constraints) gauge Lagrangian formulations with equivalent dynamics, but different configuration spaces are found. We outline within $Q_c$-approach the concept of consistent local cubic interactions and evaluate the candidate structure of cubic vertices involving $p\geq 3$ copies of interacting massless mixed-antisymmetric fields.

papers.title: TROPT: An Open Framework for Unifying and Advancing Discrete Text Optimization
papers.abstract: Discrete text-trigger optimization -- searching for text sequences that, when ingested by a model, steer it toward a specified objective -- underpins model red-teaming (e.g., LLM jailbreaks), as well as auditing and interpretability. However, the current state of discrete optimizers hinders their adoption and progress. First, existing optimizers, when open-sourced at all, are scattered across research codebases tied to specific models, objectives, and problem domains. Second, optimizers proliferate, each requiring engineering overhead to use or extend, and remaining hard to compare head-to-head. Together, these raise the bar for adopting optimizers in existing or new domains, and for advancing them via new strategies. We address these gaps with TROPT, the first open-source framework that unifies discrete optimizers' execution and standardizes their development under a single interface. TROPT makes it easy to customize end-to-end optimization recipes by swapping any component -- models, objectives, and optimizers -- extending its reach across domains and new applications. TROPT currently ships with 40+ optimization recipes -- covering applications such as jailbreaking and probing model internals -- built from 15+ optimizers (spanning white-box to black-box access) and 15+ losses, from foundational to state-of-the-art methods.
